planComparisons.title: Function filter versus a date range
planComparisons.question: Same January result, different access paths.

cases.label: Function on the indexed column
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_time ON watch_events(watched_at); SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)='2025-01';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)='2025-01';

cases.label: Half-open range
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_time ON watch_events(watched_at); SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at>='2025-01-01' AND watched_at<'2025-02-01';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at>='2025-01-01' AND watched_at<'2025-02-01';

planComparisons.takeaway: Wrapping an indexed column in a function hides it from the index, so SQLite reads every entry. A half-open range on the bare column lets it jump straight to January.
planComparisons.explain: An index stores watched_at values in sorted order, like a phone book. SQLite can jump into that order only when the WHERE clause compares the bare column to a value. strftime('%Y-%m', watched_at) produces a new value for every row, and that value is not what the index stores, so SQLite has to compute it for every entry and check each one. Rewriting the filter as watched_at >= '2025-01-01' AND watched_at < '2025-02-01' asks for a slice of the sorted order, which the index can find directly.

planComparisons.title: No supporting index versus an index
planComparisons.question: The result is unchanged; compare SCAN and SEARCH.

cases.label: Without a customer index
cases.query: SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;

cases.label: With a customer index
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_customer ON orders(customer_id); SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;

planComparisons.takeaway: Without an index SQLite must read the whole table. An index on the filtered column turns the SCAN into a SEARCH that touches only matching rows.
planComparisons.explain: Without an index, the only way to find orders for customer 1 is to read every row of the table and keep the matches: a SCAN. CREATE INDEX builds a separate sorted list of customer_id values, each pointing at its row. With it, SQLite looks up customer 1 in that list and visits only those rows: a SEARCH. The work grows with the number of matches instead of the size of the table.

planComparisons.title: Covering index
planComparisons.question: Both search the same index. Which one never touches the table?
planComparisons.takeaway: When every column the query needs is inside the index, SQLite answers from the index alone. The plan says COVERING INDEX and skips the extra lookup into the table.

cases.label: Index on the filter column only
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders(customer_id); SELECT customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;

cases.label: Index that also holds quantity
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust_qty ON orders(customer_id,quantity); SELECT customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;

planComparisons.explain: A normal index lookup is two steps: find the key in the index, then jump to the table row to fetch the other columns. If the index already contains every column the query asks for, the second step is unnecessary. Index (customer_id) holds only customer_id, so SQLite still visits the table for quantity. Index (customer_id, quantity) holds both, so the answer comes straight from the index.

planComparisons.title: Sorting with and without an index
planComparisons.question: Same ORDER BY. Does SQLite have to sort?
planComparisons.takeaway: With no suitable index, SQLite builds a temporary b-tree to sort the rows (USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY). An index already in that order lets it read rows pre-sorted, so the sort step disappears.

cases.label: No index on the sort column
cases.query: SELECT id,ordered_at FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_at;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,ordered_at FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_at;

cases.label: Index in the sort order
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_ordered ON orders(ordered_at); SELECT id,ordered_at FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_at;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,ordered_at FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_at;

planComparisons.explain: To return rows in ordered_at order, SQLite either reads them in any order and sorts them afterwards, or reads them from something that is already sorted. With no index it must collect the rows into a temporary b-tree and sort them first, which costs extra time and memory as the table grows. An index on ordered_at is already sorted, so walking it returns rows in the right order and the sort step disappears.

planComparisons.title: Column order in a composite index
planComparisons.question: Same filter on product_id, two indexes with the columns swapped.
planComparisons.takeaway: A composite index can only be searched from its leftmost column. With customer_id first, a filter on product_id alone cannot use it and SQLite scans. Putting product_id first makes it searchable.

cases.label: Index (customer_id, product_id)
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cp ON orders(customer_id,product_id); SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE product_id=2;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE product_id=2;

cases.label: Index (product_id, customer_id)
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_pc ON orders(product_id,customer_id); SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE product_id=2;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE product_id=2;

planComparisons.explain: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then by the second within each first-column value, like a phone book sorted by last name, then first name. You can find everyone named Smith quickly, but finding everyone named John means reading the whole book. Index (customer_id, product_id) is sorted by customer_id first, so a filter on product_id alone cannot use it. Index (product_id, customer_id) puts product_id first and can be searched.

planComparisons.title: Equality first, then a range
planComparisons.question: Both indexes cover customer_id and ordered_at. Which uses both columns?
planComparisons.takeaway: SQLite uses index columns left to right: any number of equality tests, then at most one range. Index (customer_id, ordered_at) uses both terms; index (ordered_at, customer_id) stops at the range and filters customer_id row by row.

cases.label: Index (customer_id, ordered_at)
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust_date ON orders(customer_id,ordered_at); SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 AND ordered_at>='2025-01-01';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 AND ordered_at>='2025-01-01';

cases.label: Index (ordered_at, customer_id)
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_date_cust ON orders(ordered_at,customer_id); SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 AND ordered_at>='2025-01-01';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 AND ordered_at>='2025-01-01';

planComparisons.explain: SQLite walks a composite index left to right. It can use any number of leading columns tested with =, then one more column tested with a range, and then it must stop. With (customer_id, ordered_at) it jumps to customer 1 and reads only that customer's dates after the cutoff. With (ordered_at, customer_id) it can only use the range on ordered_at; every order after the cutoff is read and customer_id is checked row by row.

planComparisons.title: LIKE with a leading wildcard
planComparisons.question: Same index on name. Which pattern can use it?
planComparisons.takeaway: A known prefix such as 'Be%' becomes a range (name>? AND name<?) that the index can search. A pattern starting with % could match anywhere, so every entry has to be checked. The index uses COLLATE NOCASE because SQLite's LIKE ignores case by default.

cases.label: Wildcard at the start ('%en')
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON customers(name COLLATE NOCASE); SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%en';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%en';

cases.label: Known prefix ('Be%')
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON customers(name COLLATE NOCASE); SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'Be%';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'Be%';

planComparisons.explain: A pattern that starts with known letters, such as 'Be%', describes one contiguous slice of a sorted index: everything from 'Be' up to just before 'Bf'. SQLite turns it into a range search. A pattern that starts with %, such as '%en', could match anywhere in the alphabet, so there is no slice to jump to and every entry must be checked. The index uses COLLATE NOCASE because SQLite's LIKE ignores case by default, and the index must sort the same way.

planComparisons.title: OR across two columns
planComparisons.question: customer_id = 1 OR product_id = 2. What changes when both columns are indexed?
planComparisons.takeaway: An OR is only as good as its weakest branch: if one side has no index, SQLite scans the table. When both columns are indexed it can search each index separately and combine the results (MULTI-INDEX OR).

cases.label: Only customer_id is indexed
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders(customer_id); SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 OR product_id=2;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 OR product_id=2;

cases.label: Both columns are indexed
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders(customer_id); CREATE INDEX idx_prod ON orders(product_id); SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 OR product_id=2;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 OR product_id=2;

planComparisons.explain: For customer_id = 1 OR product_id = 2, SQLite must find rows that match either side. If only customer_id is indexed, the product_id side can only be found by reading every row, and once it is reading every row anyway, it scans the table for both. When both columns are indexed, it searches each index separately and combines the two sets of rows, without reading the rest of the table.

planComparisons.title: OR versus IN on one column
planComparisons.question: Three ORs on customer_id, or one IN list. Is one faster?
planComparisons.takeaway: SQLite rewrites several ORs on the same column into an IN list, so both versions get the identical plan. Write whichever reads more clearly; the plan, not the spelling, decides the work.

cases.label: Several ORs on one column
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders(customer_id); SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 OR customer_id=2 OR customer_id=3;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 OR customer_id=2 OR customer_id=3;

cases.label: The same test written with IN
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders(customer_id); SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (1,2,3);
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (1,2,3);

planComparisons.explain: Before planning, SQLite rewrites customer_id = 1 OR customer_id = 2 OR customer_id = 3 into customer_id IN (1, 2, 3). Both forms are then planned identically: one index search per value in the list. This comparison is a reminder that the database plans the meaning of a query, not its spelling, so choose whichever form reads more clearly.

planComparisons.title: Indexing a join key
planComparisons.question: Count views per video. What does an index on the join key change?
planComparisons.takeaway: Without an index on watch_events.video_id, SQLite scans every event and needs a temporary b-tree to group them. With the index it walks the videos and searches each one's events directly, and the grouping step disappears.

cases.label: Join key without an index
cases.query: SELECT v.title,COUNT(*) AS views FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT v.title,COUNT(*) AS views FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id;

cases.label: Join key with an index
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_video ON watch_events(video_id); SELECT v.title,COUNT(*) AS views FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT v.title,COUNT(*) AS views FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id;

planComparisons.explain: To count views per video, SQLite has to pair each video with its watch events. Without an index on watch_events.video_id it reads every event, looks up its video by primary key, and then sorts the pairs in a temporary b-tree to group them by video. With the index, it walks the videos in order and searches each video's events directly. The pairs come out already grouped, so the extra sort disappears.

planComparisons.title: Index on an expression
planComparisons.question: Keep the strftime filter. Can an index still help?
planComparisons.takeaway: An ordinary index on watched_at cannot serve strftime('%Y-%m', watched_at). An index built on that exact expression can: the plan searches it with <expr>=?. Use this when you cannot rewrite the filter as a range.

cases.label: Index on the column
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_time ON watch_events(watched_at); SELECT id FROM watch_events WHERE strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)='2025-01';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM watch_events WHERE strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)='2025-01';

cases.label: Index on the expression
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_month ON watch_events(strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)); SELECT id FROM watch_events WHERE strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)='2025-01';
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id FROM watch_events WHERE strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at)='2025-01';

planComparisons.explain: Sometimes you cannot rewrite a filter as a range, for example when the application always asks by month label. SQLite can index the result of an expression instead of a column. CREATE INDEX on strftime('%Y-%m', watched_at) stores that computed label for every row in sorted order, so the same function filter becomes an index search. The expression in the query must match the indexed expression exactly.

planComparisons.title: GROUP BY with and without an index
planComparisons.question: Total units per customer. Does SQLite need a grouping step?
planComparisons.takeaway: To group, SQLite needs rows that share a key next to each other. Without an index it builds a temporary b-tree (USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY). An index on (customer_id, quantity) already holds rows in group order and covers the query.

cases.label: No index on the group key
cases.query: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

cases.label: Index (customer_id, quantity)
cases.query: CREATE INDEX idx_cq ON orders(customer_id,quantity); SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
cases.plan: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

planComparisons.explain: To total quantity per customer, SQLite needs the rows of each customer next to each other. Without an index it reads the table and builds a temporary b-tree that sorts rows by customer_id before adding them up. An index on (customer_id, quantity) already stores rows in customer order and contains quantity too, so SQLite reads groups straight from the index with no sort and without touching the table.

lessons.title: Meet your first SELECT
lessons.concept: A table is a collection of rows and named columns. SELECT chooses the columns you want to see; FROM names the table. A query reads data without changing it.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, city
FROM customers;
lessons.trap: SELECT * includes extra columns. Return only the columns the task asks for.
hints: Name the two columns after SELECT, separated by a comma.
Use FROM customers for the first challenge; FROM products for the second.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

lessons.concept: AS gives an output column a readable name. You can calculate values for each row with arithmetic. The original table stays unchanged.
lessons.example:

FROM products;
lessons.trap: AS names the result. It does not update the stored column. A quoted number is text, so use a numeric expression for arithmetic.
hints: Use multiplication in SELECT.
Use AS to name the calculated column exactly as requested.

lessons.title: Unique values with DISTINCT
lessons.concept: DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows. It applies to the whole set of selected columns, not just the first column. NULL is kept once.
lessons.example:
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM customers;
lessons.trap: Adding id makes every row unique, so it defeats this task.
hints: Add DISTINCT directly after SELECT.
Select just the column whose unique values you want.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

lessons.title: Filter with WHERE
lessons.concept: WHERE keeps rows for which a condition is true. Text values need single quotes; column names do not. Rows whose comparison evaluates to NULL are not kept.

WHERE city = 'Chicago';
lessons.trap: SQL uses = for equality. City names are string values, so quote them.
hints: Use WHERE city = a quoted city.
Return only name and city.

tasks.prompt: Show name and price for Tech products costing less than 100.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,price FROM products WHERE category='Tech' AND price<100

tasks.prompt: Show name and price for Home or Stationery products costing at least 12.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,price FROM products WHERE (category='Home' OR category='Stationery') AND price>=12

quiz.q: Which rows does category = 'Tech' AND price < 100 keep?
options: Every Tech product, plus anything priced under 100
Products that are both Tech and priced under 100
Products that are Tech or priced under 100
quiz.why: AND requires both conditions on the same row. OR would keep a row that meets either one.

walkthrough.title: Require both conditions
walkthrough.description: Category and price are separate columns. AND keeps a row only when both are true.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, category, price FROM products;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: AND requires both conditions. OR requires either. AND binds more tightly than OR, so parentheses make mixed conditions explicit.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE category = 'Tech' AND price < 100;

lessons.title: Lists & text patterns
lessons.concept: IN matches any member of a list. LIKE matches text patterns: % means any number of characters and _ means one character. SQLite LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII by default.
lessons.example:
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';
lessons.trap: An equality comparison with A% looks for a literal percent sign.
hints: A prefix pattern ends with %.
Use IN with a parenthesized list of quoted cities.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show name for customers whose name starts with A.
tasks.answer: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'A%'

tasks.prompt: Show name and city for customers in Austin or Seattle.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,city FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Austin','Seattle')

quiz.q: What does name LIKE 'A%' match?
options: Names that contain a percent sign
quiz.why: In LIKE, % stands for any number of characters. An equality comparison would look for a literal percent sign.

walkthrough.title: Match the start of a name
walkthrough.description: In LIKE, % stands for the rest of the name. It is not a character stored in the table.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name FROM customers;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: IN matches any member of a list. LIKE matches text patterns: % means any number of characters and _ means one character. SQLite LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII by default.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

lessons.title: Understand NULL
lessons.concept: NULL means missing or unknown. NULL = NULL is unknown, not true. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city
FROM customers;
lessons.trap: NULL is not the string 'NULL', and it is not an empty string.
hints: Do not use = NULL.
Use IS NULL to find missing values, or COALESCE to replace them.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show name for customers whose city is missing.
tasks.answer: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL

tasks.prompt: Return name and city, replacing missing city with Unknown (alias the column city).
tasks.answer: SELECT name,COALESCE(city,'Unknown') AS city FROM customers

quiz.q: What happens when WHERE city = NULL is evaluated?
options: The comparison is unknown; those rows are not kept
quiz.why: Use IS NULL for missing values. Ordinary comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown.

walkthrough.title: Find missing cities
walkthrough.description: Some city values are blank in the sense of NULL. Equality to NULL never matches; IS NULL does.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL;

walkthrough.title: Replace NULL for display
walkthrough.description: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. Missing cities become the label Unknown without changing stored rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city FROM customers;

lessons.title: Sort & limit
lessons.concept: ORDER BY sorts the output; ASC is ascending and DESC descending. LIMIT keeps a number of rows after sorting. Use a secondary key when ties need deterministic ordering.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, price FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC LIMIT 3;
lessons.trap: LIMIT without ORDER BY does not promise which rows you get.
hints: Sort by price, then use LIMIT.
Most expensive needs DESC; cheapest needs ASC.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show name and price of the 3 most expensive products, highest price first.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3

tasks.prompt: Show name and price of the 2 cheapest products, lowest price first.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,price FROM products ORDER BY price ASC LIMIT 2

quiz.q: How do you return the three cheapest products consistently?
quiz.why: Ascending price puts cheaper products first. id breaks equal-price ties; LIMIT keeps three rows.

walkthrough.title: Sort prices before cutting
walkthrough.description: ORDER BY decides which rows come first. LIMIT only makes sense after the sort, or you get an arbitrary cut.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC;

walkthrough.title: Keep the top of the sorted list
walkthrough.description: DESC puts expensive products first. LIMIT 3 keeps only the first three after sorting.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC LIMIT 3;

lessons.title: COUNT, SUM & AVG
lessons.concept: Aggregate functions collapse rows into a summary. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) excludes NULL. SUM adds numeric values; AVG finds their mean.
lessons.example:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers;
lessons.trap: COUNT(city) excludes Elena because her city is NULL.
hints: An aggregate query without GROUP BY returns one summary row.
Use COUNT(*) for rows or SUM(quantity) for units.
lessons.grain: One row per requested summary group.

tasks.prompt: Return the number of customers as customer_count.
tasks.answer: SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM customers

tasks.prompt: Return total order quantity as total_units.
tasks.answer: SELECT SUM(quantity) AS total_units FROM orders

quiz.q: A table has three rows, and one city is NULL. What do COUNT(*) and COUNT(city) return?
quiz.why: COUNT(*) counts every row. COUNT(city) counts only rows with a non-NULL city.

walkthrough.title: Look at the rows being counted
walkthrough.description: Each customer is one row. An aggregate without GROUP BY collapses the whole table into one summary.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name FROM customers;

walkthrough.title: Collapse to a single count
walkthrough.description: COUNT(*) counts rows. SUM and AVG work the same way: many input rows become one summary value.
walkthrough.query: SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM customers;

lessons.title: Group into summaries
lessons.concept: GROUP BY forms one group for each key. Aggregates then summarize each group. Select grouping columns and aggregates to avoid ambiguous output.
lessons.example:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM products GROUP BY category;
lessons.trap: Selecting an ungrouped name in SQLite can return an arbitrary member of the group.
hints: Put the grouping key after GROUP BY.
Use COUNT(*) or SUM(quantity) for the summary column.
lessons.grain: One row per requested summary group.

tasks.prompt: Show category and product_count for each product category.
tasks.answer: SELECT category,COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category

tasks.prompt: Show status and total_units (sum of quantity) for each order status.
tasks.answer: SELECT status,SUM(quantity) AS total_units FROM orders GROUP BY status

quiz.q: Products belong to two categories. What is the grain after GROUP BY category?
options: Always one row for the whole table
quiz.why: GROUP BY forms one group per category. Each output row summarizes that category.

walkthrough.title: Read product rows
walkthrough.description: Two products belong to each category. The input grain is one product.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,name,category FROM products;

walkthrough.title: Count within groups
walkthrough.description: GROUP BY changes the grain to one category.
walkthrough.query: SELECT category,COUNT(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category;

lessons.title: Filter groups with HAVING
lessons.concept: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Think rows → groups → group filter → output.
lessons.trap: WHERE cannot filter an aggregate computed by the same query block.
hints: Filter the aggregate in HAVING.
The aggregate expression must match the summary you are testing.
lessons.grain: One row per requested summary group.

tasks.prompt: Show customer_id and order_count for customers with at least 2 orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT customer_id,COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*)>=2

tasks.prompt: Show customer_id and total_units for customers with total quantity greater than 3.
tasks.answer: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS total_units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity)>3

quiz.q: Which clause keeps only groups whose total quantity is greater than 10?
quiz.why: HAVING filters after aggregates are calculated. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.

walkthrough.title: Form groups first
walkthrough.description: GROUP BY customer_id builds one row per customer with an order_count. HAVING will filter these groups next.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Keep only qualifying groups
walkthrough.description: HAVING runs after aggregation. It removes groups whose aggregate fails the test, unlike WHERE which filters source rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

lessons.title: Make decisions with CASE
lessons.concept: CASE creates a value based on conditions. SQL checks WHEN branches in order and uses the first match. ELSE covers remaining rows.
lessons.trap: Without ELSE, unmatched rows become NULL.
hints: CASE WHEN condition THEN value ELSE value END.
Add AS tier or AS is_paid.
lessons.grain: One row per requested summary group.

tasks.prompt: Show name and tier: Premium if price >= 80, otherwise Standard.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,CASE WHEN price>=80 THEN 'Premium' ELSE 'Standard' END AS tier FROM products

tasks.prompt: Show id and is_paid: 1 for paid orders, otherwise 0.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_paid FROM orders

quiz.q: If no WHEN condition matches a CASE expression, what does ELSE supply?
options: A filter that removes the row
quiz.why: CASE chooses a value for each row. ELSE is the fallback when no WHEN condition is true.

walkthrough.title: Read the prices you will classify
walkthrough.description: Each product has a price. CASE will label rows at or above 80 as Premium and the rest as Standard.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price;

walkthrough.title: Assign a tier with CASE
walkthrough.description: WHEN branches are checked in order. The first true branch wins; ELSE covers everything else.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, CASE WHEN price >= 80 THEN 'Premium' ELSE 'Standard' END AS tier FROM products;

lessons.title: Conditional aggregation
lessons.concept: Put CASE inside SUM to count or add only matching rows. ELSE 0 prevents nonmatching rows from contributing. This can produce multiple summaries in one scan.
lessons.example:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid'
THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_count FROM orders;
lessons.trap: COUNT(CASE ... ELSE 0 END) counts zero values too because they are not NULL.
hints: Wrap CASE in SUM.
Return 1 to count a row; return quantity to sum units.
lessons.grain: One row per requested summary group.

tasks.prompt: Return paid_count: the number of paid orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_count FROM orders

tasks.prompt: Return paid_units: the sum of quantity for paid orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN quantity ELSE 0 END) AS paid_units FROM orders

quiz.q: What does SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) count?
quiz.why: Each paid row contributes one; other rows contribute zero. The aggregate adds those contributions.

walkthrough.title: See paid vs other statuses
walkthrough.description: Orders mix paid and unpaid statuses. Conditional aggregation can count only the paid ones in one pass.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, status, quantity FROM orders ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Count only paid rows inside SUM
walkthrough.description: CASE returns 1 for paid rows and 0 otherwise. SUM adds those values into paid_count.
walkthrough.query: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_count FROM orders;

lessons.title: Connect tables with JOIN
lessons.concept: INNER JOIN pairs rows whose join condition matches. Aliases keep column references short. One customer can match several orders, so joins can increase row counts.
lessons.example:
SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
lessons.trap: Joining without the correct ON condition can multiply unrelated rows.
hints: Match the foreign key in orders to the other table's id.
Use table aliases to distinguish the two id columns.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return every order id and its customer name (columns id, name).
tasks.answer: SELECT o.id,c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id

tasks.prompt: Return every order id and its product name (columns id, name).
tasks.answer: SELECT o.id,p.name FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id

quiz.q: What does an INNER JOIN do with a customer who has no matching order?
options: Keeps the customer with NULL order columns
Leaves the customer out of the joined result
Invents an order for the customer
quiz.why: INNER JOIN returns matching pairs only. A customer with several matching orders appears once for each match.

walkthrough.title: Find the matching keys
walkthrough.description: orders.customer_id references customers.id. Read both columns so the JOIN condition is concrete before you write it.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id AS order_id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Combine matching rows with JOIN
walkthrough.description: INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that satisfy the ON condition. Aliases keep the two id columns clear.
walkthrough.query: SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;

lessons.title: Keep unmatched rows
lessons.concept: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table. When no match exists, right-side columns are NULL. A right-table filter in WHERE may remove those unmatched rows.
lessons.trap: Using INNER JOIN loses Hugo, who has no orders.
hints: Customers must be on the left side.
COUNT(o.id) ignores NULL; COUNT(*) would count the unmatched placeholder row.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show every customer name and order_count, including customers with zero orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT c.name,COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id,c.name

tasks.prompt: Show name for customers with no orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL

quiz.q: After a LEFT JOIN, how do you count zero orders for a customer with no match?
quiz.why: The customer row is preserved, but o.id is NULL. COUNT(o.id) ignores that NULL and returns zero.

walkthrough.title: Identify the preserved side
walkthrough.description: Every customer must stay, even Hugo without an order.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM customers;

walkthrough.title: Inspect the joined rows
walkthrough.description: Customers repeat for each order. Hugo gets a NULL right-side id.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.id,c.name,o.id AS order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id;

walkthrough.title: Count matching right-side ids
walkthrough.description: COUNT(o.id) ignores the unmatched NULL and gives Hugo zero.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.name,COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id,c.name;

lessons.title: Revenue across tables
lessons.concept: Join transaction rows to product prices, multiply price by quantity, then aggregate at the desired grain. Filter status before computing paid revenue.
lessons.example:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id
WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name;
lessons.trap: Summing price without quantity undercounts multi-unit orders.
hints: Revenue per order is quantity * price.
Join products on product_id and filter to paid before grouping.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show customer name and paid revenue (alias revenue), only customers with paid orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT c.name,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name

tasks.prompt: Show category and paid revenue (alias revenue) for each category with paid orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT p.category,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category

quiz.q: What does quantity * price compute for one paid order line?
options: The customer's lifetime value across all orders
That line's revenue before you aggregate by customer or category
The number of products in the order
quiz.why: Each order row is one product line. Multiplying quantity by price gives that line's revenue; SUM and GROUP BY then produce a total at the grain you choose.

walkthrough.title: Read an order line with its price
walkthrough.description: Join one order line to its product so quantity and price sit on the same row. The next step multiplies them and aggregates paid revenue.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT o.id, o.quantity, p.price, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: Join transaction rows to product prices, multiply price by quantity, then aggregate at the desired grain. Filter status before computing paid revenue.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id
JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id
WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name;

lessons.title: Subqueries
lessons.concept: A subquery is a query inside another query. A scalar subquery produces one value, which can be used in a comparison. Parentheses separate the inner query.
lessons.example:
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
lessons.trap: The inner average summarizes the entire table; it is not a per-row calculation.
hints: Calculate the average with an inner SELECT.
Use > followed by the parenthesized subquery.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show name and price of products above the average product price.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,price FROM products WHERE price>(SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)

tasks.prompt: Show id and quantity for orders whose quantity is above the average order quantity.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE quantity>(SELECT AVG(quantity) FROM orders)

quiz.q: In price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products), what does the inner query supply?
options: One average price used by the outer comparison
Every product row joined to the outer query
quiz.why: AVG without GROUP BY produces one summary value. The outer query compares each product price with that value.

walkthrough.title: Compute the comparison value
walkthrough.description: A subquery can produce the average price once. The outer query will compare each product to that single number.
walkthrough.query: SELECT AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM products;

walkthrough.title: Filter rows against the subquery
walkthrough.description: The parenthesized SELECT runs as a scalar subquery. Rows with price above that average remain.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);

lessons.title: Ask whether a row exists
lessons.concept: EXISTS is true when its subquery returns at least one row. A correlated subquery refers to the outer row. NOT EXISTS is useful for finding missing relationships.
lessons.trap: A join may duplicate customer names; EXISTS preserves one outer row.
hints: Correlate customer_id to the outer customer id.
Use EXISTS for at least one, NOT EXISTS for none.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Show name of customers who have at least one paid order.
tasks.answer: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid')

tasks.prompt: Show name of customers who have no paid orders.
tasks.answer: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid')

quiz.q: What does NOT EXISTS test for each outer row?
options: Whether the subquery finds no matching rows
Whether every selected value is NULL
Whether the outer table is empty
quiz.why: NOT EXISTS is true when the correlated subquery returns no rows. It tests existence, not the value selected.

walkthrough.title: Check for a matching paid order
walkthrough.description: EXISTS asks whether at least one related row satisfies the inner filter. It does not multiply the outer customer rows.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.status FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY c.id LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Keep customers with a match
walkthrough.description: EXISTS returns true when the correlated subquery finds one or more rows. The outer SELECT lists those customers once.
walkthrough.query: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid');

lessons.title: Combine sets with UNION
lessons.concept: UNION stacks compatible query outputs and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL retains duplicates. Both sides need the same number of columns in matching positions.
lessons.example:
SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city='Chicago'
UNION SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city='Austin';
lessons.trap: UNION combines rows vertically; JOIN combines columns horizontally.
hints: Stack SELECT statements using UNION or UNION ALL.
The output column name comes from the first SELECT.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return distinct city values from Chicago customers and Austin customers using UNION.
tasks.answer: SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city='Chicago' UNION SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city='Austin'

tasks.prompt: Stack name from customers and name from products, keeping duplicates.
tasks.answer: SELECT name FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT name FROM products

quiz.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION removes duplicate result rows; UNION ALL keeps them
UNION ALL sorts the rows automatically
UNION combines columns instead of rows
quiz.why: Both combine compatible result rows. UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL preserves them.

walkthrough.title: Build two compatible city lists
walkthrough.description: Chicago and Austin rows each produce a city column. UNION stacks compatible selects and drops duplicates.
walkthrough.query: SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Chicago', 'Austin') ORDER BY city;

walkthrough.title: Stack sets with UNION
walkthrough.description: UNION removes duplicates across the stacked rows. UNION ALL would keep every duplicate.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Chicago'
UNION SELECT city FROM customers WHERE city = 'Austin';

lessons.title: Readable queries with CTEs
lessons.concept: WITH names a temporary query result for this statement. Common table expressions help you separate a complicated question into understandable stages. They do not create permanent tables.
lessons.trap: A CTE exists only for the statement that follows it.
hints: Define the intermediate result with WITH name AS (...).
The outer query filters the named result.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Use a CTE to return customer_id and units for customers whose total quantity exceeds 3.
tasks.answer: WITH totals AS(SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id,units FROM totals WHERE units>3

tasks.prompt: Use a CTE to return category and avg_price for categories with average price greater than 30.
tasks.answer: WITH averages AS(SELECT category,AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM products GROUP BY category) SELECT category,avg_price FROM averages WHERE avg_price>30

quiz.q: What does WITH totals AS (...) create?
options: A permanent table saved for later queries
A named query result available within this statement
An index on the source table
quiz.why: A common table expression names a query result for the current statement. It does not create a permanent table.

walkthrough.title: Name an intermediate total
walkthrough.description: WITH defines a temporary result you can read like a table. Here each customer gets a units total before filtering.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Filter the named CTE
walkthrough.description: The outer query reads totals as if it were a table. CTEs make multi-step logic easier to follow than nested subqueries.

lessons.title: Window functions: ROW_NUMBER
lessons.concept: Window functions calculate across related rows while keeping each row visible. ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3 within a partition using its ORDER BY. Include a tie-breaker for repeatable results.
lessons.trap: The window ORDER BY controls calculation, not the final display order.
hints: PARTITION BY restarts numbering per group.
Put ORDER BY inside OVER to control numbering.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return id, customer_id and order_number: number each customer's orders by ordered_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at,id) AS order_number FROM orders

tasks.prompt: Return name, category and price_rank: number products within category by price descending then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,category,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS price_rank FROM products

quiz.q: What does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at, id) do?
options: Collapses each customer to one row
Numbers each customer’s rows from 1, keeping every row
Uses one numbering sequence for all customers
quiz.why: PARTITION BY starts a new sequence for each customer. ORDER BY sets the sequence; id breaks equal timestamps.

walkthrough.title: Order a customer's orders
walkthrough.description: ROW_NUMBER needs a clear order within each partition. Sort one customer's orders by time to see the sequence.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY ordered_at, id;

walkthrough.title: Number rows inside each partition
walkthrough.description: PARTITION BY customer_id restarts the counter for each customer. ORDER BY decides which row is 1, 2, 3…

lessons.title: RANK & DENSE_RANK
lessons.concept: RANK gives ties the same rank, then leaves a gap. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps. ROW_NUMBER always assigns distinct numbers.
lessons.trap: Ties exist in this dataset, so RANK and DENSE_RANK produce different outputs.
hints: Aggregate counts first; rank those grouped rows.
Do not put customer_id in the window sort: that would break count ties.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Show customer_id, order_count and rank using DENSE_RANK by order_count descending.
tasks.answer: SELECT customer_id,COUNT(*) AS order_count,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rank FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

tasks.prompt: Show customer_id, order_count and rank using RANK by order_count descending.
tasks.answer: SELECT customer_id,COUNT(*) AS order_count,RANK() OVER(ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rank FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id

quiz.q: For tied values 100, 100, 90, what do RANK and DENSE_RANK assign to 90?
quiz.why: RANK leaves a gap after a tie. DENSE_RANK counts distinct ranked values without gaps.

walkthrough.title: Measure the value you will rank
walkthrough.description: Ranking needs a sort key. Count orders per customer first; DENSE_RANK will order those counts.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY order_count DESC, customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Assign dense ranks to groups
walkthrough.description: DENSE_RANK gives the same rank to ties and does not skip the next rank. RANK would leave gaps after ties.

lessons.title: Running totals
lessons.concept: SUM as a window function keeps each row and accumulates values over a frame. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means all earlier rows plus this row.
lessons.trap: Specify a ROWS frame to avoid a default RANGE frame grouping equal sort values.
hints: Use SUM(quantity) OVER (...).
The second task needs PARTITION BY customer_id.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Show id, quantity and running_units: cumulative quantity ordered by ordered_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,quantity,SUM(quantity) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_units FROM orders

tasks.prompt: Show id, customer_id and running_units: cumulative quantity per customer ordered by ordered_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,SUM(quantity) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_units FROM orders

quiz.q: What does a running SUM with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW include?
options: This row and every earlier row in the sort order
quiz.why: UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through CURRENT ROW accumulates every row so far. It counts rows in the frame, not a fixed number of days.

walkthrough.title: Keep every order in order
walkthrough.description: A running total still returns each order. The frame adds this row to the rows before it.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, quantity, ordered_at FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_at, id;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: SUM as a window function keeps each row and accumulates values over a frame. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means all earlier rows plus this row.

lessons.title: Compare rows with LAG
lessons.concept: LAG reads a value from a previous row within a window. The first row has no predecessor, so its result is NULL unless you supply a default.
lessons.trap: LAG uses the window ordering; it is not the previous row in storage.
hints: The argument of LAG is the value you want from the previous row.
Subtract LAG(quantity) from quantity to calculate change.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Show id, customer_id and previous_quantity for the previous order of each customer, ordered by ordered_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,LAG(quantity) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at,id) AS previous_quantity FROM orders

tasks.prompt: Show id, quantity and change: current quantity minus previous quantity across all orders, ordered by ordered_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,quantity,quantity-LAG(quantity) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_at,id) AS change FROM orders

quiz.q: What does LAG(value) return for the first row in a partition when no default is supplied?
options: The last value in the partition
quiz.why: There is no previous row at the start of a partition, so LAG returns NULL unless you supply a default.

walkthrough.title: Line up a customer's quantities
walkthrough.description: LAG looks at the previous row in the same partition. Sorting by time makes previous mean the prior order.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, quantity, ordered_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY ordered_at, id;

walkthrough.title: Read the previous quantity
walkthrough.description: LAG(quantity) returns the prior order's quantity for that customer. The first order has NULL for previous.

lessons.title: Latest row per group
lessons.concept: Use a CTE with ROW_NUMBER sorted newest-first, then filter to row number 1. A window result cannot be filtered by WHERE in the same query block.
lessons.trap: MAX(date) plus an unrelated id does not reliably select the entire latest row.
hints: Number rows inside a CTE, then filter outside it.
Keep rn = 1 in the outer WHERE.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return id, customer_id and ordered_at for the latest order per customer; break date ties by highest id.
tasks.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM orders) SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_at FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

tasks.prompt: Return name, category and price for the most expensive product per category; break price ties by lowest id.
tasks.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS rn FROM products) SELECT name,category,price FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

quiz.q: How do you keep one latest row per customer with ROW_NUMBER?
options: Number all rows globally and keep the first
Partition by customer, order newest first with a tie-breaker, then filter rn = 1 in an outer query
quiz.why: Partitioning separates customers. Ordering identifies the latest row; an outer query filters the window result.

walkthrough.title: See multiple rows per customer
walkthrough.description: Customers can have several orders. Choosing the latest one needs an order and a way to keep only rank 1.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered_at FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, ordered_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Keep the newest row per group
walkthrough.description: ROW_NUMBER ordered by newest first marks the latest order as 1. Filtering rn = 1 keeps one row per customer.

lessons.title: Dates & monthly analysis
lessons.concept: SQLite stores these dates as ISO text. strftime formats dates: %Y-%m extracts a year and month. Group by that expression to build a monthly summary. Other SQL dialects use different date functions.
lessons.example:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_at) AS month,
COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY month;
lessons.trap: Grouping only by month number mixes years.
hints: Use strftime with %Y-%m.
Filter paid rows before grouping for the second task.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and order_count for all orders by month.
tasks.answer: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',ordered_at) AS month,COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY month

tasks.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and paid_units for paid orders by month.
tasks.answer: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',ordered_at) AS month,SUM(quantity) AS paid_units FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY month

quiz.q: What does GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_at) produce?
options: One row per calendar year and month
One row per year, ignoring the month
quiz.why: %Y-%m keeps the year and month together. Grouping by the month number alone would mix the same month from different years.

walkthrough.title: Read the order dates
walkthrough.description: Each order has one timestamp. The next step groups those timestamps into year-month buckets.
walkthrough.query: SELECT ordered_at FROM orders;

walkthrough.title: Run the reference
walkthrough.description: SQLite stores these dates as ISO text. strftime formats dates: %Y-%m extracts a year and month. Group by that expression to build a monthly summary. Other SQL dialects use different date functions.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_at) AS month,
COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY month;

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.concept: A recursive CTE has an anchor row and a recursive step joined by UNION ALL. The step uses the previous result until its stopping condition is false. Always include a termination condition.
lessons.trap: An unbounded recursive query is interrupted by the app time limit.
hints: Anchor with SELECT 1.
Increment n and stop at the requested upper bound.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Use a recursive CTE to return n with integers 1 through 5.
tasks.answer: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS(SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers

tasks.prompt: Use a recursive CTE to return n with integers 1 through 10.
tasks.answer: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS(SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<10) SELECT n FROM numbers

quiz.q: Which part of a recursive CTE supplies the starting rows?
quiz.why: The anchor supplies the starting rows. The recursive part derives subsequent rows from the current result.

walkthrough.title: Start from a base row
walkthrough.description: A recursive CTE needs an anchor member. Here the sequence begins at 1 before the recursive step adds 1.
walkthrough.query: SELECT 1 AS n;

walkthrough.title: Grow the sequence recursively
walkthrough.description: UNION ALL attaches rows produced from previous rows until the WHERE stop condition fails.

lessons.title: Query plans & indexes
lessons.concept: An index can help SQLite find or order rows efficiently. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows SCAN versus SEARCH and index use. Indexes cost storage and slow writes; the optimizer may still scan a tiny table.
lessons.example:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city='Chicago';
lessons.trap: A full scan is not automatically bad; table size and selectivity matter.
hints: Write the SELECT normally; choose Explain for its plan.
Plan output is informative; submit the normal query to check the answer.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Show name for Chicago customers. Run the reference with Explain mode to inspect the plan.
tasks.answer: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city='Chicago'

tasks.prompt: Show id and quantity for paid orders. Inspect its plan with Explain mode.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE status='paid'

quiz.q: What does EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN show?
options: The exact number of milliseconds every future run will take
quiz.why: A plan shows how SQLite intends to access data. It does not measure execution time or prove a production speedup.

walkthrough.title: Run the filtered lookup
walkthrough.description: This is the query whose plan you will inspect. Note the city predicate—indexes may later speed this path.
walkthrough.query: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Chicago';

walkthrough.title: Read the query plan
walkthrough.description: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN names the access strategy (scan, search, and so on). Indexes change which path the engine picks.
walkthrough.query: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Chicago';

lessons.title: Capstone: customer insights
lessons.concept: Combine filtering, joins, aggregation and ranking to answer a business question. First compute each customer's paid revenue, then rank those customer totals. Write one stage at a time.
lessons.trap: Rank customer totals, not individual order amounts.
hints: Compute paid revenue in a grouped CTE.
Rank the revenue column in the outer query.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Show name, paid_revenue and revenue_rank for customers with paid orders. Use DENSE_RANK, highest revenue first in the rank calculation.
tasks.answer: WITH revenue AS(SELECT c.name,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS paid_revenue FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name) SELECT name,paid_revenue,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY paid_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank FROM revenue

tasks.prompt: Show category, paid_revenue and revenue_rank for product categories with paid orders. Use DENSE_RANK by revenue descending.
tasks.answer: WITH revenue AS(SELECT p.category,SUM(o.quantity*p.price) AS paid_revenue FROM orders o JOIN products p ON p.id=o.product_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category,paid_revenue,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY paid_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank FROM revenue

quiz.q: Why calculate customer revenue before ranking customers?
options: To rank one total per customer instead of individual order lines
To remove all customers with tied totals
quiz.why: The reporting grain is one customer. Aggregate order-line revenue to that grain before ranking.

walkthrough.title: Assemble paid revenue pieces
walkthrough.description: Customer insights join customers, paid orders, and product prices before summing. Check the join keys first.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT c.name, o.quantity, p.price, o.status
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Summarize paid revenue per customer
walkthrough.description: The capstone CTE pattern computes paid_revenue, then the outer query ranks or filters those totals.
walkthrough.query:
WITH revenue AS (
  SELECT c.name, SUM(o.quantity * p.price) AS paid_revenue
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = o.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY c.name
) SELECT name, paid_revenue FROM revenue ORDER BY paid_revenue DESC;

lessons.title: MIN, MAX & the grain of a result
lessons.concept: MIN and MAX summarize the smallest and largest values. The grain describes what one output row means. Adding GROUP BY changes that grain from one overall row to one row per group.
lessons.example:
SELECT MIN(watch_seconds) AS shortest_watch,
MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events;
lessons.trap: A maximum value alone does not identify every other column from that row.
hints: Decide whether the task wants one overall row or one row per video.
Use MIN and MAX; put video_id in GROUP BY for the second task.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return shortest_watch and longest_watch: minimum and maximum watch_seconds across all watch events.
tasks.answer: SELECT MIN(watch_seconds) AS shortest_watch,MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events

tasks.prompt: Return video_id and longest_watch: maximum watch_seconds for each video that has events.
tasks.answer: SELECT video_id,MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events GROUP BY video_id

quiz.q: What is the grain of SELECT MIN(price), MAX(price) FROM products without GROUP BY?
options: One summary row for the whole input
quiz.why: Aggregates without GROUP BY summarize the input into one row. MIN and MAX find the lowest and highest values.

walkthrough.title: Scan the watch lengths
walkthrough.description: Each event has watch_seconds. One overall MIN/MAX summarizes the whole table; GROUP BY later changes the grain.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, video_id, watch_seconds FROM watch_events ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;

walkthrough.title: Summarize at the overall grain
walkthrough.description: Without GROUP BY, MIN and MAX return one row for the entire result. That grain is “the whole table.”
walkthrough.query: SELECT MIN(watch_seconds) AS shortest_watch, MAX(watch_seconds) AS longest_watch FROM watch_events;

lessons.title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
lessons.concept: NOT reverses true and false, but unknown stays unknown. If a NOT IN list contains NULL, a nonmatching comparison can become unknown and disappear from WHERE. Prefer NOT EXISTS for nullable relationships.
lessons.trap: Filtering NULL out of the subquery or using NOT EXISTS avoids the unknown-value trap.
hints: The nullable referred_by column makes a bare NOT IN unsafe.
Correlate the inner referred_by to the outer viewer id with NOT EXISTS.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return id for viewers who have not referred anyone. A referred_by value identifies the referrer, and NULL means no referrer.
tasks.answer: SELECT v.id FROM viewers v WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM viewers r WHERE r.referred_by=v.id)

tasks.prompt: Return id and country for viewers outside US and GB.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,country FROM viewers WHERE country NOT IN('US','GB')

quiz.q: Why can NOT IN (SELECT nullable_key ...) unexpectedly return no rows?
options: NULL can turn nonmatching comparisons into unknown
quiz.why: Unknown does not pass WHERE. Filter NULLs from the list or use NOT EXISTS.

walkthrough.title: Inspect nullable relationships
walkthrough.description: NULL here means no referring viewer.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,referred_by FROM viewers;

walkthrough.title: See the NOT IN trap
walkthrough.description: A NULL in this subquery makes NOT IN unknown for nonmatches. Observe the empty result.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id FROM viewers WHERE id NOT IN(SELECT referred_by FROM viewers);

walkthrough.title: Use an existence test
walkthrough.description: NOT EXISTS asks whether a matching referring relationship is absent.
walkthrough.query: SELECT v.id FROM viewers v WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM viewers r WHERE r.referred_by=v.id);

lessons.title: Ratios, ROUND & NULLIF
lessons.concept: A rate is numerator divided by denominator. Use a real number (100.0) to avoid integer division. NULLIF(x,0) turns a zero denominator into NULL; ROUND controls displayed precision. Preserve that NULL instead of calling an undefined rate zero.
lessons.trap: COUNT(*) in a LEFT JOIN makes an account with no requests appear to have one request.
hints: Count requests, not placeholder rows produced by LEFT JOIN.
Use 100.0 * successes / NULLIF(COUNT(r.id),0) for all accounts.
lessons.grain: One row per requested summary group.

tasks.prompt: Return account_id and success_pct (0–100, rounded to 2 decimals) for accounts with requests.
tasks.answer: SELECT account_id,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN status='success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(COUNT(*),0),2) AS success_pct FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id

tasks.prompt: Return id and success_pct for every account, including accounts with no requests (NULL rate). Round to 2 decimals.
tasks.answer: SELECT a.id,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN r.status='success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(COUNT(r.id),0),2) AS success_pct FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id GROUP BY a.id

quiz.q: What does NULLIF(denominator, 0) do when the denominator is zero?
options: Returns NULL so a ratio can represent an undefined result
quiz.why: NULLIF returns NULL when its arguments are equal. Division by that missing denominator produces NULL rather than a meaningful ratio.

walkthrough.title: Count successes and attempts
walkthrough.description: A success rate needs both numerator and denominator. NULLIF protects against dividing by zero.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT account_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS successes,
  COUNT(*) AS attempts
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id;

walkthrough.title: Turn counts into a rounded percent
walkthrough.description: Multiply by 100.0 for a real division, wrap the denominator in NULLIF(..., 0), then ROUND to two decimals.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT account_id, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'success' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS success_pct
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id;

lessons.title: Clean strings & cast values
lessons.concept: TRIM removes outside spaces, LOWER normalizes case, SUBSTR extracts a portion, and CAST makes a conversion explicit. Keep NULL visible when the source is missing. SQLite uses SUBSTR; many engines also provide SUBSTRING.
lessons.example: SELECT id,LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email FROM members;
lessons.trap: Normalizing email is useful for analysis, but changing a real identity field needs business rules.
hints: Nest LOWER around TRIM.
INSTR finds @; SUBSTR starts one character after it.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return id and clean_email for every member: trim outside spaces and lowercase the email; preserve NULL.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email FROM members

tasks.prompt: Return id and email_domain: lowercase, trim, and take the email text after @. Preserve NULL.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,SUBSTR(LOWER(TRIM(email)),INSTR(TRIM(email),'@')+1) AS email_domain FROM members

quiz.q: Why apply TRIM before comparing a text identifier?
options: To remove leading and trailing spaces
To remove every space inside the identifier
To convert all text to a number
quiz.why: TRIM removes surrounding spaces. It keeps internal spaces; case normalization and type conversion are separate operations.

walkthrough.title: See messy emails before cleaning
walkthrough.description: Whitespace and mixed case make the same address look different. Cleaning must happen before you compare or group.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, email FROM members ORDER BY id LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Normalize with TRIM and LOWER
walkthrough.description: TRIM removes surrounding spaces; LOWER folds case. Together they produce a stable clean_email.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS clean_email FROM members;

lessons.title: Self-joins & referral relationships
lessons.concept: A self-join uses the same table in two roles. Use different aliases for the member and referrer. LEFT JOIN retains members who were not referred.
lessons.example:
SELECT m.id AS member_id,r.id AS referrer_id
FROM members m LEFT JOIN members r ON r.id=m.referrer_id;
lessons.trap: The member’s country and the referrer’s country are different attributes.
hints: The same table can appear twice with different aliases.
Join referrer.id to member.referrer_id.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return member_id and referrer_id for every member, keeping NULL when no referrer exists.
tasks.answer: SELECT m.id AS member_id,r.id AS referrer_id FROM members m LEFT JOIN members r ON r.id=m.referrer_id

tasks.prompt: Return member_id and referrer_country for members with a referrer, taking the country from the referrer row.
tasks.answer: SELECT m.id AS member_id,r.country AS referrer_country FROM members m JOIN members r ON r.id=m.referrer_id

quiz.q: How does a self-join distinguish the two roles of the same table?
options: By giving each occurrence a different alias
By renaming the stored table twice
quiz.why: Aliases let you refer to the same table as different roles, such as employee and manager or customer and referrer.

walkthrough.title: Read members and their referrer ids
walkthrough.description: referrer_id points at another row in the same table. A self-join uses two aliases for those two roles.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, email, country, referrer_id FROM members ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Join the table to itself
walkthrough.description: Alias m is the member and r is the referrer. LEFT JOIN keeps members who have no referrer.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT m.id AS member_id, r.id AS referrer_id
FROM members m LEFT JOIN members r ON r.id = m.referrer_id;

lessons.title: CROSS JOIN & a complete date grid
lessons.concept: CROSS JOIN creates every pair of rows. It is useful for a deliberate date × entity grid, but careless use multiplies data. The three dates below are supplied setup data via a VALUES list—you are not being tested on UNION. Focus on CROSS JOIN (and optional signup filtering).
lessons.trap: The expected grid size is dates × viewers before the signup filter.
hints: Treat the VALUES date list as given setup data, then CROSS JOIN viewers.
Filter day >= signup_at after creating the grid for the second task.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return day and viewer_id for every day from 2025-01-01 through 2025-01-03 inclusive and every viewer, including pre-signup combinations.
tasks.answer: SELECT day,v.id AS viewer_id FROM (SELECT column1 AS day FROM (VALUES ('2025-01-01'), ('2025-01-02'), ('2025-01-03'))) AS days CROSS JOIN viewers v

tasks.prompt: Return day and viewer_id for the same date range, keeping only combinations on or after that viewer's signup_at.
tasks.answer: SELECT day,v.id AS viewer_id FROM (SELECT column1 AS day FROM (VALUES ('2025-01-01'), ('2025-01-02'), ('2025-01-03'))) AS days CROSS JOIN viewers v WHERE day>=v.signup_at

quiz.q: How many combinations does a CROSS JOIN of two customers and three dates produce?
quiz.why: A CROSS JOIN pairs every row on one side with every row on the other: two times three combinations.

walkthrough.title: Use the provided three dates
walkthrough.description: These three day values are setup data (a VALUES list). You do not need UNION or recursion—your job is the CROSS JOIN next.

walkthrough.title: Pair every date with every viewer
walkthrough.description: CROSS JOIN multiplies the date list by the viewers. Filter by signup_at only after the grid exists when the task asks for that.

lessons.title: FULL OUTER JOIN & unmatched records
lessons.concept: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. Reconciliation often needs this to find missing records. This SQLite version supports FULL OUTER JOIN; older SQLite versions did not.
lessons.example:
SELECT i.id AS invoice_id,p.id AS payment_id
FROM invoices i FULL OUTER JOIN payments p ON p.invoice_id=i.id;
lessons.trap: Split payments make one invoice match more than one payment.
hints: Use FULL OUTER JOIN for retaining both sides.
A missing invoice match has i.id IS NULL.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return invoice_id and payment_id for every invoice/payment match, retaining unmatched rows on either side. Keep split payments as separate rows.
tasks.answer: SELECT i.id AS invoice_id,p.id AS payment_id FROM invoices i FULL OUTER JOIN payments p ON p.invoice_id=i.id

tasks.prompt: Return payment_id for payments whose invoice_id has no matching invoice, including NULL invoice_id.
tasks.answer: SELECT p.id AS payment_id FROM payments p LEFT JOIN invoices i ON i.id=p.invoice_id WHERE i.id IS NULL

quiz.q: Which unmatched rows does a FULL OUTER JOIN preserve?
options: Only unmatched rows on the left
Only unmatched rows on the right
quiz.why: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps matching pairs and unmatched rows from either side, filling the other side with NULL.

walkthrough.title: See invoice and payment keys
walkthrough.description: Some invoices lack payments and some payments lack invoices. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

walkthrough.title: Retain unmatched rows on both sides
walkthrough.description: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matches plus leftovers from either table. Missing matches show NULL on the empty side.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT i.id AS invoice_id, p.id AS payment_id
FROM invoices i FULL OUTER JOIN payments p ON p.invoice_id = i.id;

lessons.title: ON versus WHERE in a LEFT JOIN
lessons.concept: ON decides which right-side rows may match. WHERE filters the joined output. Put a success condition in ON when you need to keep accounts with no successful requests.
lessons.trap: A WHERE r.status filter discards unmatched accounts and changes the result.
hints: Keep accounts on the left and status in the ON condition.
COUNT(r.id), not COUNT(*), represents matching requests.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return id and successful_requests for every account, including zero successful requests.
tasks.answer: SELECT a.id,COUNT(r.id) AS successful_requests FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id AND r.status='success' GROUP BY a.id

tasks.prompt: Return id and error_requests for every account, including zero failed requests (status = error).
tasks.answer: SELECT a.id,COUNT(r.id) AS error_requests FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id AND r.status='error' GROUP BY a.id

quiz.q: Why can WHERE o.status = 'paid' after a LEFT JOIN remove customers with no orders?
options: Their right-side status is NULL, so the condition is not true
quiz.why: WHERE filters the joined result. A condition on the right side rejects the unmatched NULL row; put a match restriction in ON when every customer must remain.

walkthrough.title: The dangerous filter
walkthrough.description: Filtering success in WHERE loses the account without successful requests.
walkthrough.query: SELECT a.id,COUNT(r.id) AS successful_requests FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id WHERE r.status='success' GROUP BY a.id;

walkthrough.title: Filter matching rows in ON
walkthrough.description: All accounts stay; only successful requests can match.
walkthrough.query: SELECT a.id,COUNT(r.id) AS successful_requests FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN ai_requests r ON r.account_id=a.id AND r.status='success' GROUP BY a.id;

lessons.title: INTERSECT & EXCEPT
lessons.concept: INTERSECT keeps distinct rows appearing in both results. EXCEPT keeps distinct rows from the first result that are absent from the second. Column positions and types should align.
lessons.example:
SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=1
INTERSECT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=2;
lessons.trap: UNION means either set, which answers a different question.
hints: Build one set of viewer ids for each video.
INTERSECT is both; EXCEPT is first minus second.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return viewer_id for viewers who watched both video 1 and video 2. Each viewer appears once.
tasks.answer: SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=1 INTERSECT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=2

tasks.prompt: Return viewer_id for viewers who watched video 1 but never video 2. Each viewer appears once.
tasks.answer: SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=1 EXCEPT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id=2

quiz.q: What does A EXCEPT B return?
options: Distinct rows in A that are absent from B
quiz.why: EXCEPT subtracts the right result from the left and returns distinct remaining rows.

walkthrough.title: List viewers of video 1
walkthrough.description: INTERSECT will keep viewers who also watched video 2. EXCEPT would keep viewers of video 1 who never watched video 2.
walkthrough.query: SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id = 1 ORDER BY viewer_id;

walkthrough.title: Keep viewers in both sets
walkthrough.description: INTERSECT returns distinct rows present in both SELECT results. Column positions must align.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id = 1
INTERSECT SELECT viewer_id FROM watch_events WHERE video_id = 2;

lessons.title: Date boundaries & monthly buckets
lessons.concept: For timestamps, use a half-open interval: >= start and < next boundary. This includes every time on the last day without guessing the final second. SQLite uses strftime/date; PostgreSQL uses DATE_TRUNC and INTERVAL. All teaching timestamps are UTC.
lessons.example:
SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events
WHERE watched_at >= '2025-01-01' AND watched_at < '2025-02-01';
lessons.trap: BETWEEN with an end date at midnight can omit that date’s later events.
hints: End at the first instant of the next month, using <.
Format the timestamp to year-month before grouping.
lessons.grain: One row per entity or event requested by the task.

tasks.prompt: Return id and watched_at for January 2025 watch events, including the full final day and excluding February.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at>='2025-01-01' AND watched_at<'2025-02-01'

tasks.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and active_viewers (distinct viewers) across all watch events by month.
tasks.answer: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',watched_at) AS month,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers FROM watch_events GROUP BY month

quiz.q: Which range includes every January timestamp and excludes February?
quiz.why: A half-open interval handles the full last day and excludes the next boundary.

walkthrough.title: Bound January with half-open dates
walkthrough.description: Timestamps need a clear start and end. Use >= month start and < next month start so the boundary stays unambiguous.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at >= '2025-01-01' AND watched_at < '2025-02-01' ORDER BY watched_at LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Select the January window
walkthrough.description: The half-open range includes midnight on January 1 and excludes midnight on February 1.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at >= '2025-01-01' AND watched_at < '2025-02-01';

lessons.title: LEAD & the next event
