lessons.concept: LEAD looks forward within a partition. Use it to see the next event or compute a gap. The last row has no next event and returns NULL. Deterministic ordering needs a tie-breaker.
lessons.trap: Using global rather than per-viewer order compares unrelated people.
hints: Put LEAD(watched_at) inside a viewer partition.
unixepoch converts a timestamp to integer seconds for subtraction.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return id, viewer_id and next_watch_at for each viewer's next watch event, ordering each viewer by watched_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,viewer_id,LEAD(watched_at) OVER(PARTITION BY viewer_id ORDER BY watched_at,id) AS next_watch_at FROM watch_events

tasks.prompt: Return id and seconds_to_next: next watched_at minus current watched_at in seconds per viewer, ordered by watched_at then id. Last events get NULL.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,unixepoch(LEAD(watched_at) OVER(PARTITION BY viewer_id ORDER BY watched_at,id))-unixepoch(watched_at) AS seconds_to_next FROM watch_events

quiz.q: What does LEAD(value) return when there is no next row and no default is supplied?
quiz.why: LEAD reads the next row in the ordered partition. At the end, it returns NULL unless a default is supplied.

walkthrough.title: Order a viewer's watch timeline
walkthrough.description: LEAD looks forward in the same partition. Sort one viewer's events by time to see what “next” means.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, viewer_id, watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE viewer_id = 1 ORDER BY watched_at, id;

walkthrough.title: Read the next event time
walkthrough.description: LEAD(watched_at) returns the following event's timestamp for that viewer. The last event has NULL for next.

lessons.title: FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE & frames
lessons.concept: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE read endpoints of a window frame. LAST_VALUE with the default ordered frame often returns the current row. Use UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to reach the final row in the partition.
lessons.trap: The default frame is not always the entire partition.
hints: For LAST_VALUE the frame must include future rows.
Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return id, viewer_id and last_video for each viewer's final watched video, ordered within viewer by watched_at then id. Repeat that final video on every viewer row.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,viewer_id,LAST_VALUE(video_id) OVER(PARTITION BY viewer_id ORDER BY watched_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_video FROM watch_events

tasks.prompt: Return id, viewer_id and first_video for each viewer's first watched video, ordered within viewer by watched_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,viewer_id,FIRST_VALUE(video_id) OVER(PARTITION BY viewer_id ORDER BY watched_at,id) AS first_video FROM watch_events

quiz.q: Why does LAST_VALUE often return the current row?
options: The default ordered frame may end at the current row
It only works with one row
quiz.why: Extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to include the final row in the partition.

walkthrough.title: Follow one viewer's video sequence
walkthrough.description: LAST_VALUE needs an explicit frame to see the end of the partition as rows accumulate.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, viewer_id, video_id, watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE viewer_id = 1 ORDER BY watched_at, id;

walkthrough.title: Carry the last video with a frame
walkthrough.description: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING lets LAST_VALUE see the whole partition for each row.

lessons.title: Rolling averages & missing dates
lessons.concept: A rolling average smooths variation. ROWS counts rows, not calendar days. When dates are missing, a three-row average differs from a three-day average. Fill missing days with zero only if the business definition says absence means no activity.
lessons.trap: Three rows are not three days when dates are missing.
hints: For a three-row frame use 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
For calendar days, generate a complete date spine and join metrics before the window.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return day, watch_minutes and rolling_avg (2 decimals) for the current and previous 2 observed rows in daily_metrics, sorted by day. This task intentionally uses rows, not calendar days.
tasks.answer: SELECT day,watch_minutes,ROUND(AVG(watch_minutes) OVER(ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS rolling_avg FROM daily_metrics ORDER BY day

tasks.prompt: Return day, watch_minutes and rolling_avg (2 decimals) for every day Jan 1–7 2025, treating absent daily_metrics days as zero. Average current and previous 2 calendar days; early windows use available days. Sort by day.
tasks.answer: WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS(SELECT '2025-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day,'+1 day') FROM days WHERE day<'2025-01-07'), complete AS(SELECT d.day,COALESCE(m.watch_minutes,0) AS watch_minutes FROM days d LEFT JOIN daily_metrics m ON m.day=d.day) SELECT day,watch_minutes,ROUND(AVG(watch_minutes) OVER(ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS rolling_avg FROM complete ORDER BY day

quiz.q: Does ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW always represent three calendar days?
options: Yes, whenever there is ORDER BY
Only when there is one complete row per calendar day
No, it always includes all preceding rows
quiz.why: ROWS counts rows. Missing dates require a complete date spine for a calendar-day window.

walkthrough.title: Notice missing dates
walkthrough.description: Jan 3 and Jan 6 are absent. A row frame skips those dates.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM daily_metrics ORDER BY day;

walkthrough.title: Average observed rows
walkthrough.description: For Jan 4, the frame is Jan 1, Jan 2, Jan 4. That is three rows, not three calendar days.
walkthrough.query: SELECT day,watch_minutes,ROUND(AVG(watch_minutes) OVER(ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS rolling_avg FROM daily_metrics ORDER BY day

walkthrough.title: Build a complete calendar
walkthrough.description: Missing days become zero under the explicit business rule.
walkthrough.query: WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS(SELECT '2025-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day,'+1 day') FROM days WHERE day<'2025-01-07') SELECT d.day,COALESCE(m.watch_minutes,0) AS watch_minutes FROM days d LEFT JOIN daily_metrics m ON m.day=d.day ORDER BY d.day;

walkthrough.title: Average calendar days
walkthrough.description: Now each row is one day. The frame’s three rows are also three days.
walkthrough.query: WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS(SELECT '2025-01-01' UNION ALL SELECT date(day,'+1 day') FROM days WHERE day<'2025-01-07'), complete AS(SELECT d.day,COALESCE(m.watch_minutes,0) AS watch_minutes FROM days d LEFT JOIN daily_metrics m ON m.day=d.day) SELECT day,watch_minutes,ROUND(AVG(watch_minutes) OVER(ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW),2) AS rolling_avg FROM complete ORDER BY day

lessons.title: Share of total with windows
lessons.concept: An aggregate window without GROUP BY can put a grand total alongside each group. Aggregate per model first, then use SUM(request_count) OVER() as the denominator.
lessons.example:
WITH counts AS(SELECT model,COUNT(*) AS request_count
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY model)
SELECT model,request_count,ROUND(100.0*request_count/
SUM(request_count) OVER(),2) AS share_pct FROM counts;
lessons.trap: Partitioning by model would give each model 100%.
hints: Compute one row per model in a CTE.
SUM(...) OVER() returns the grand total without collapsing model rows.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return model, request_count and share_pct (0–100, 2 decimals) for all request rows by model.
tasks.answer: WITH counts AS(SELECT model,COUNT(*) AS request_count FROM ai_requests GROUP BY model) SELECT model,request_count,ROUND(100.0*request_count/SUM(request_count) OVER(),2) AS share_pct FROM counts

tasks.prompt: Return model, output_tokens and share_pct (0–100, 2 decimals) of total successful output tokens by model.
tasks.answer: WITH totals AS(SELECT model,SUM(output_tokens) AS output_tokens FROM ai_requests WHERE status='success' GROUP BY model) SELECT model,output_tokens,ROUND(100.0*output_tokens/NULLIF(SUM(output_tokens) OVER(),0),2) AS share_pct FROM totals

quiz.q: Why use SUM(value) OVER () as the denominator for share of total?
options: It repeats the overall total while keeping each detail row
It collapses all rows into one
It selects only the largest value
quiz.why: The window aggregate exposes the total on each row. Divide each row’s value by that total, using appropriate numeric and zero-denominator handling.

walkthrough.title: Count requests per model
walkthrough.description: A share of total needs each group's count and the grand total. Start from the per-model counts.
walkthrough.query: SELECT model, COUNT(*) AS request_count FROM ai_requests GROUP BY model ORDER BY model;

walkthrough.title: Divide each count by the window total
walkthrough.description: A window SUM over the model counts supplies the denominator so each row can show its share.

lessons.title: Deduplicate event retries
lessons.concept: Ingestion retries can produce several physical rows for one logical event. Define the event key and which version wins. ROW_NUMBER per event_key, ordered by ingested_at and id descending, keeps the latest version.
lessons.trap: DISTINCT on all columns cannot remove retries whose id or ingested_at changed.
hints: The partition is the logical event_key, not member_id.
Filter rn=1 before counting events.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return id, event_key and member_id for the latest ingested row of each event_key. Break ingestion ties by highest id.
tasks.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events) SELECT id,event_key,member_id FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

tasks.prompt: After keeping the latest ingested row per event_key (tie: highest id), return event_type and event_count by event_type.
tasks.answer: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events) SELECT event_type,COUNT(*) AS event_count FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 GROUP BY event_type

quiz.q: Why deduplicate retries by a stable event identifier before counting events?
options: Retries can otherwise count the same logical event more than once
Every repeated value is necessarily a retry
Deduplication makes every event happen on the same date
quiz.why: Multiple source versions can represent one logical event. A declared identifier and deterministic version order choose one record.

walkthrough.title: Find event retries
walkthrough.description: Logical event a has more than one physical row.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM social_events WHERE event_key='a' ORDER BY ingested_at,id;

walkthrough.title: Number versions
walkthrough.description: The latest ingestion wins; id breaks timestamp ties.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,event_key,ingested_at,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events ORDER BY event_key,rn;

walkthrough.title: Keep one version
walkthrough.description: DISTINCT on all columns cannot remove retries whose id or ingested_at changed.
walkthrough.query: WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_key ORDER BY ingested_at DESC,id DESC) AS rn FROM social_events) SELECT id,event_key,member_id FROM ranked WHERE rn=1

lessons.title: Daily active users & engagement
lessons.concept: DAU counts distinct people with activity on a calendar day, not event rows. Define engagement separately: here it is total seconds divided by active viewers. This result includes observed dates only.
lessons.example:
SELECT date(watched_at) AS day,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id)
AS active_viewers FROM watch_events GROUP BY day;
lessons.trap: Counting rows inflates activity for viewers who watched more than once.
hints: A viewer can have several watch events on the same day.
Use COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) and convert seconds to minutes with 60.0.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return day (YYYY-MM-DD) and active_viewers (distinct viewers) for every observed watch date.
tasks.answer: SELECT date(watched_at) AS day,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers FROM watch_events GROUP BY day

tasks.prompt: Return day, active_viewers and minutes_per_active_viewer, rounded to 2 decimals, for each observed watch date.
tasks.answer: SELECT date(watched_at) AS day,COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers,ROUND(SUM(watch_seconds)/60.0/COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id),2) AS minutes_per_active_viewer FROM watch_events GROUP BY day

quiz.q: One viewer watches three videos on the same day. How much do they contribute to daily active viewers?
options: Zero unless all videos are different
quiz.why: Daily active viewers counts DISTINCT viewer_id for the day. Watch events and engagement seconds are separate measures.

walkthrough.title: Bucket watches by calendar day
walkthrough.description: Daily active users need a day grain. date(watched_at) turns timestamps into calendar days before counting viewers.
walkthrough.query: SELECT date(watched_at) AS day, viewer_id FROM watch_events ORDER BY day, viewer_id LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Count distinct viewers per day
walkthrough.description: COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) counts people, not events. Grouping by day produces the DAU series.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT date(watched_at) AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT viewer_id) AS active_viewers
FROM watch_events GROUP BY date(watched_at);

lessons.title: Ordered conversion funnels
lessons.concept: A funnel is an ordered journey. Find the first view, then the first signup on or after that view, then the first purchase on or after signup. A purchase that happens before signup does not complete this funnel. Equal timestamps are allowed here.
lessons.example:
-- Build one row per member at each stage.
WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS viewed,COUNT(signed_at) AS signed_up,
COUNT(purchased_at) AS purchased FROM funnel;
lessons.trap: Counting event types independently ignores sequence and includes invalid journeys.
hints: Make the next step conditional on the previous step’s timestamp.
Use LEFT JOIN for stage counts so drop-offs remain in the denominator.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return one row: viewed, signed_up, purchased as member counts for the ordered view → signup → purchase funnel. Equal times are allowed; use each member's earliest valid next step.
tasks.answer: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT COUNT(*) AS viewed,COUNT(signed_at) AS signed_up,COUNT(purchased_at) AS purchased FROM funnel

tasks.prompt: Return member_id, viewed_at, signed_at and purchased_at for members who complete that ordered funnel.
tasks.answer: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT member_id,viewed_at,signed_at,purchased_at FROM funnel WHERE purchased_at IS NOT NULL

quiz.q: A person purchases before signing up, then never purchases again. Did they finish the ordered signup → purchase funnel?
options: No, the purchase must occur on or after signup
quiz.why: Sequence is part of the metric definition. Independent event counts cannot establish an ordered journey.

walkthrough.title: Find first views
walkthrough.description: The denominator is members who entered the funnel.
walkthrough.query: SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id;

walkthrough.title: Reconstruct valid stages
walkthrough.description: Observe member 3: the purchase before view is ignored, and a later valid purchase is kept.
walkthrough.query: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT * FROM funnel;

walkthrough.title: Count people at each stage
walkthrough.description: LEFT JOIN leaves NULL at stages where a person drops off.
walkthrough.query: WITH views AS(SELECT member_id,MIN(event_at) AS viewed_at FROM social_events WHERE event_type='view' GROUP BY member_id), signups AS(SELECT v.member_id,v.viewed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS signed_at FROM views v LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=v.member_id AND e.event_type='signup' AND e.event_at>=v.viewed_at GROUP BY v.member_id,v.viewed_at), funnel AS(SELECT s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at,MIN(e.event_at) AS purchased_at FROM signups s LEFT JOIN social_events e ON e.member_id=s.member_id AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=s.signed_at GROUP BY s.member_id,s.viewed_at,s.signed_at) SELECT COUNT(*) AS viewed,COUNT(signed_at) AS signed_up,COUNT(purchased_at) AS purchased FROM funnel

lessons.title: Cohorts & exact-day retention
lessons.concept: A cohort groups people by signup date. Exact-day D1 retention asks whether they return on signup +1 day, not anytime later. Count people, include non-returners, and exclude cohorts that have not matured by the observation cutoff.
lessons.example:
-- D1 retention; observation cutoff is 2025-01-15
SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-1 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at
lessons.trap: A seven-day window and exact-day D7 retention are different metrics.
hints: The denominator is all viewers in the mature signup cohort.
Use EXISTS on the exact return date to avoid duplicating viewers.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: With observation cutoff Jan 15 2025, return cohort_day, cohort_size, retained_viewers and retention_pct (0–100, 2 decimals) for exact-day D1 retention. Include only mature cohorts.
tasks.answer: SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+1 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-1 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

tasks.prompt: Use the same output and cutoff for exact-day D7 retention (signup date +7 days); include only mature cohorts.
tasks.answer: SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

quiz.q: Exact-day D7 retention means a user returns when?
options: Any time during the first seven days
On signup date plus seven calendar days
quiz.why: Exact-day, rolling-window, and unbounded retention use different definitions.

walkthrough.title: Define mature cohorts
walkthrough.description: Each row is one viewer in a cohort that can have a D7 observation.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,signup_at,date(signup_at,'+7 days') AS return_day FROM viewers WHERE signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days');

walkthrough.title: Mark exact-day returns
walkthrough.description: EXISTS counts each person at most once, even if several events occur on the return date.
walkthrough.query: SELECT v.id,v.signup_at,CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS retained FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days');

walkthrough.title: Report D7 retention
walkthrough.description: Retained people divided by all mature cohort members.
walkthrough.query: SELECT v.signup_at AS cohort_day,COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained_viewers,ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM watch_events w WHERE w.viewer_id=v.id AND date(w.watched_at)=date(v.signup_at,'+7 days')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*),2) AS retention_pct FROM viewers v WHERE v.signup_at<=date('2025-01-15','-7 days') GROUP BY v.signup_at

lessons.title: Sessionize an event stream
lessons.concept: A session starts on a member’s first event or after a gap of at least 30 minutes. LAG finds the prior timestamp, CASE flags boundaries, and a running SUM numbers sessions. Here we use physical rows, including retries. Identical timestamps do not start a new session.
lessons.trap: Strictly greater than 30 minutes is not the same as at least 30 minutes.
hints: Use unixepoch differences in seconds to avoid floating date rounding.
Mark gaps >=1800 seconds, then running SUM the markers per member.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Using raw social_events, return member_id and session_count. Start a new session on the first event or a gap of at least 30 minutes; order by event_at then id per member.
tasks.answer: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT member_id,MAX(session_number) AS session_count FROM numbered GROUP BY member_id

tasks.prompt: Using the same rule, return id, member_id and session_number for every raw social event.
tasks.answer: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT id,member_id,session_number FROM numbered

quiz.q: With a gap rule of at least 30 minutes, does a 30-minute gap start a new session?
quiz.why: The boundary is inclusive. Integer timestamp differences keep that definition precise.

walkthrough.title: Find the previous timestamp
walkthrough.description: Order within member. Raw retries remain in this exercise.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id,member_id,event_at,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events ORDER BY member_id,event_at,id;

walkthrough.title: Number the sessions
walkthrough.description: A new boundary occurs on the first event or a gap >=1800 seconds.
walkthrough.query: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT id,member_id,session_number FROM numbered

walkthrough.title: Summarize sessions per member
walkthrough.description: The largest session number is the total number of sessions.
walkthrough.query: WITH previous AS(SELECT *,LAG(event_at) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id) AS previous_at FROM social_events), marked AS(SELECT *,CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL OR unixepoch(event_at)-unixepoch(previous_at)>=1800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session FROM previous), numbered AS(SELECT *,SUM(new_session) OVER(PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_number FROM marked) SELECT member_id,MAX(session_number) AS session_count FROM numbered GROUP BY member_id

lessons.title: Multi-grain joins without fan-out
lessons.concept: Requests and invoices each have many rows per account. Joining raw tables creates requests × invoices and inflates sums. Aggregate each side to one row per account before joining; keep accounts with zero on either side.
lessons.example:
WITH usage AS(SELECT account_id,COUNT(*) AS request_count
FROM ai_requests GROUP BY account_id), billing AS(
SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount
FROM invoices GROUP BY account_id)
SELECT a.id,COALESCE(u.request_count,0) AS request_count,
COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount FROM ai_accounts a
LEFT JOIN usage u ON u.account_id=a.id
LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id;
lessons.trap: DISTINCT cannot repair inflated SUM values after a many-to-many join.
hints: Choose account as the grain for both intermediate tables.
Join the summaries to accounts only after GROUP BY account_id.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

quiz.q: Why aggregate requests and invoices separately before joining account totals?
options: To prevent each request from matching every invoice and multiplying totals
To discard accounts with more than one request
To force every account total to be equal
quiz.why: Both child tables can have several rows per account. Aggregating each to one row per account avoids many-to-many fan-out.

lessons.title: Revenue & payment reconciliation
lessons.concept: Reconciliation compares independent totals. Sum payments and refunds by invoice before joining. Net collected is payments minus refunds; gap is billed minus net collected. A refund creates a gap under this definition, even when the original bill was paid.
lessons.example:
WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM refunds GROUP BY invoice_id)
SELECT i.id,i.billed_amount,
COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)-COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS net_collected,
i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap
FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id
LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id;
lessons.trap: Unmatched payments need a separate investigation; they are not assigned to an invoice here.
hints: Aggregate the two transaction tables independently.
A split payment combined with two refunds produces four joined rows unless pre-aggregated.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return id, billed_amount, net_collected and gap for every invoice across all periods. Net collected = payments - refunds; gap = billed - net collected. Treat missing totals as zero.
tasks.answer: WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM refunds GROUP BY invoice_id) SELECT i.id,i.billed_amount,COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)-COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS net_collected,i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id

tasks.prompt: Using the same definition, return invoice_id and gap only for invoices with nonzero gap.
tasks.answer: WITH paid AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_amount FROM payments GROUP BY invoice_id),returned AS(SELECT invoice_id,SUM(amount) AS refund_amount FROM refunds GROUP BY invoice_id), result AS(SELECT i.id AS invoice_id,i.billed_amount-COALESCE(p.paid_amount,0)+COALESCE(r.refund_amount,0) AS gap FROM invoices i LEFT JOIN paid p ON p.invoice_id=i.id LEFT JOIN returned r ON r.invoice_id=i.id) SELECT invoice_id,gap FROM result WHERE gap<>0

quiz.q: Why keep invoice totals separate from payment totals before reconciliation?
options: Invoices and payments can have different row grains
Every invoice always has exactly one payment
Joining raw rows always preserves both sums
quiz.why: An invoice can have multiple payments. Summarize each source at the reconciliation grain before comparing totals.

lessons.title: AI usage cost & contribution margin
lessons.concept: Usage cost equals input tokens × input rate plus output tokens × output rate, divided by one million. These rates are fictional. Under this exercise’s rule, successful requests are chargeable; errors are excluded. Compare January billed revenue to January successful usage cost, not all-time billing.
lessons.example:
SELECT r.model,ROUND(SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+
r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0,6) AS usage_cost
FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model
WHERE r.status='success' GROUP BY r.model;
lessons.trap: This simplified contribution margin excludes other costs and refunds; it is not net profit.
hints: Rates are per million; divide after adding input and output charges.
Summarize both usage and billing per account before joining.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return model and usage_cost in fictional USD, rounded to 6 decimals, for successful requests across all dates.
tasks.answer: SELECT r.model,ROUND(SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0,6) AS usage_cost FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model WHERE r.status='success' GROUP BY r.model

tasks.prompt: Return id, billed_amount, usage_cost and contribution_margin for every account for Jan 2025. Use January invoices and successful requests only; missing totals are zero. Round cost and margin to 6 decimals. Margin = billed - usage cost.
tasks.answer: WITH costs AS(SELECT r.account_id,SUM(r.input_tokens*m.input_per_million+r.output_tokens*m.output_per_million)/1000000.0 AS usage_cost FROM ai_requests r JOIN model_rates m ON m.model=r.model WHERE r.status='success' AND r.requested_at>='2025-01-01' AND r.requested_at<'2025-02-01' GROUP BY r.account_id),billing AS(SELECT account_id,SUM(billed_amount) AS billed_amount FROM invoices WHERE period='2025-01' GROUP BY account_id) SELECT a.id,COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0) AS billed_amount,ROUND(COALESCE(c.usage_cost,0),6) AS usage_cost,ROUND(COALESCE(b.billed_amount,0)-COALESCE(c.usage_cost,0),6) AS contribution_margin FROM ai_accounts a LEFT JOIN costs c ON c.account_id=a.id LEFT JOIN billing b ON b.account_id=a.id

quiz.q: Is billed revenue minus model token cost the same as net profit?
options: No; other costs and refunds may still be excluded
quiz.why: This exercise defines a simplified contribution margin. It does not include all operating costs.

lessons.title: Experiment conversion denominators
lessons.concept: Compare assigned members, including people who do nothing. A conversion is at least one purchase on or after assignment, through Jan 31. Counting purchases instead of members or using only active members biases the denominator. This query estimates rates, not statistical significance.
lessons.example:
WITH results AS(SELECT a.member_id,a.variant,CASE WHEN EXISTS(
 SELECT 1 FROM social_events e WHERE e.member_id=a.member_id
 AND e.event_type='purchase' AND e.event_at>=a.assigned_at
 AND e.event_at<'2025-02-01') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted
FROM experiment_assignments a)
SELECT variant,COUNT(*) AS assigned,SUM(converted) AS converted,
ROUND(100.0*SUM(converted)/COUNT(*),2) AS conversion_pct
FROM results GROUP BY variant;
lessons.trap: A higher observed conversion rate alone does not establish a significant treatment effect.
hints: Keep the assignments table as the population.
EXISTS counts a member once regardless of purchase row count.
lessons.grain: Define the business unit before joining and counting.

tasks.prompt: Return variant, assigned, converted and conversion_pct (0–100, 2 decimals). A member converts with any purchase on/after assigned_at and before Feb 1 2025. Include all assigned members.

options: Only users who opened the app
All assigned users in the defined population
quiz.why: Include assigned users who do nothing. Restricting the denominator to active users can bias the comparison.

lessons.title: Top N per group & ties
lessons.concept: Aggregate watched seconds per video, then rank videos within creator. ROW_NUMBER gives an exact N with a tie-breaker; DENSE_RANK includes ties and may return more than N. Make the tie policy explicit.
lessons.example:
WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,
SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v
JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),
ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id
ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,video_id) AS rn FROM totals)
SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2;
lessons.trap: Adding video_id to a DENSE_RANK ordering eliminates watch-time ties.
hints: Aggregate per video before ranking within creator.
Use a video_id tie-breaker only when you need an exact number of rows.
lessons.grain: Window calculations preserve the specified row grain.

tasks.prompt: Return creator_id, video_id and watch_seconds for the top 2 watched videos per creator, excluding videos with no events. Rank by total seconds descending, break ties by smallest video_id.
tasks.answer: WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,video_id) AS rn FROM totals) SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2

tasks.prompt: Return creator_id, video_id and watch_seconds for each creator's most-watched video(s), including ties. Exclude videos with no events.

quiz.q: To return exactly two rows per group with deterministic tie handling, which function fits?
quiz.why: ROW_NUMBER assigns unique positions. A stable tie-breaker determines which tied rows occupy the two positions; rank functions can include more rows when ties are kept.

walkthrough.description: Top-N per group needs a partition. Aggregate watch time per video, then number videos within each creator.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT v.creator_id, v.id AS video_id, SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds
FROM videos v JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id = v.id
GROUP BY v.creator_id, v.id
ORDER BY v.creator_id, watch_seconds DESC;

walkthrough.title: Keep the top rows per group
walkthrough.description: ROW_NUMBER or RANK inside the creator partition selects the top videos. Ties need an explicit rule.
walkthrough.query:
WITH totals AS(SELECT v.creator_id,v.id AS video_id,
SUM(w.watch_seconds) AS watch_seconds FROM videos v
JOIN watch_events w ON w.video_id=v.id GROUP BY v.id,v.creator_id),
ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY creator_id
ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,video_id) AS rn FROM totals)
SELECT creator_id,video_id,watch_seconds FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2;

lessons.title: Databases, schemas, tables & keys
lessons.concept: SQL is the language; the database engine executes it. Tables contain rows and typed columns. A primary key identifies one row; a foreign key points to another table — for example, orders.customer_id points at customers.id. To read columns from both tables in one result, match those keys with JOIN: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer_name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id. The next lesson practices joins in depth; here you use the pattern once so the key relationship is concrete. SQLite catalogs differ from SQL Server schemas. In this app each worker creates an in-memory SQLite database.
lessons.example:
SELECT name,type FROM sqlite_schema
WHERE type='table' AND name IN('customers','products','orders');
lessons.trap: A matching-looking name is not a reliable join key; use the defined identifiers.
hints: Metadata describes the database objects. sqlite_schema lists tables.
For challenge 2, JOIN orders to customers on orders.customer_id = customers.id and alias the columns order_id and customer_name.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.prompt: Return name and type for the customers, products and orders tables from sqlite_schema.
tasks.answer: SELECT name,type FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='table' AND name IN('customers','products','orders')

tasks.prompt: Return order_id and customer_name by joining orders.customer_id to customers.id for every order.
tasks.answer: SELECT o.id AS order_id,c.name AS customer_name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id

quiz.q: What does a foreign key describe?
options: A relationship from a column to a key in another table
A name for every numeric column
quiz.why: A foreign key links records to a referenced key. With enforcement enabled, an invalid reference is rejected.

FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LIMIT 8;

lessons.title: Logical query processing & row grain
lessons.concept: Think FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. This is a logical model, not a promise about physical execution. Row expressions preserve rows, aggregates collapse them, and windows add context without collapsing.
lessons.trap: SQLite accepts some alias usages other engines reject. Prefer clear expressions or an outer query for portable SQL.
hints: WHERE excludes unpaid rows before either calculation.
GROUP BY reduces rows; SUM OVER(PARTITION BY ...) preserves each paid order.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.answer: SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(quantity)>2 ORDER BY units DESC,customer_id

quiz.q: When are row conditions in WHERE applied relative to GROUP BY?
quiz.why: The logical flow filters source rows with WHERE before grouping them. HAVING then filters the groups.

walkthrough.description: One row is one paid order line.

lessons.title: CAST, text types & NULL arithmetic
lessons.concept: CAST changes a value’s representation. SQLite uses type affinity rather than SQL Server’s strict column-type model. CAST alone is not validation: nonnumeric text can become zero. NULL propagates through arithmetic unless a business rule replaces it.
lessons.example: SELECT id,CAST(price AS TEXT) AS price_text FROM lab_items;
lessons.trap: Do not assume CAST rejects malformed data; validate source text first.
hints: Use CAST(value AS TEXT) for an explicit conversion.
ABS returns magnitude without a negative sign.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.prompt: Return id and price_text by casting price to TEXT for every lab item.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,CAST(price AS TEXT) AS price_text FROM lab_items

tasks.prompt: Return id and absolute_gap as ABS(price - 50) for every lab item.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,ABS(price-50) AS absolute_gap FROM lab_items

quiz.q: What does adding a number to NULL produce?
quiz.why: NULL represents missing or unknown data. Arithmetic with NULL remains NULL; use an explicit policy before substituting a value.

walkthrough.title: Read numeric prices as stored
walkthrough.description: CAST changes how a value is represented in the result. The stored price stays numeric until you cast it.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, price FROM lab_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Cast price to text
walkthrough.description: CAST(price AS TEXT) returns a text form for display or concatenation. It is not validation by itself.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, CAST(price AS TEXT) AS price_text FROM lab_items;

lessons.title: NTILE & balanced ranking buckets
lessons.concept: NTILE divides an ordered partition into a requested number of buckets. Bucket row counts differ by at most one, with larger buckets first. It may separate equal values; use a deterministic tie-breaker if that is acceptable.
lessons.example:
SELECT id,watch_seconds,NTILE(4) OVER(
ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,id) AS bucket FROM watch_events;
lessons.trap: NTILE creates roughly equal row counts, not equal numeric ranges or tie-preserving ranks.
hints: NTILE is a window function.
PARTITION BY restarts buckets for each viewer in the second challenge.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.prompt: Return id, watch_seconds and bucket using NTILE(4), ordered within the window by watch_seconds descending then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,watch_seconds,NTILE(4) OVER(ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC,id) AS bucket FROM watch_events

tasks.prompt: Return id, viewer_id and bucket using NTILE(2) per viewer, ordered within viewer by watched_at then id.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,viewer_id,NTILE(2) OVER(PARTITION BY viewer_id ORDER BY watched_at,id) AS bucket FROM watch_events

quiz.q: What does NTILE(3) do to six ordered rows?
options: Assigns them to three buckets of two rows each
Returns only the first three rows
quiz.why: NTILE divides the ordered rows into roughly equal buckets while keeping the rows visible. When six rows divide evenly into three buckets, each gets two.

walkthrough.title: Sort the values you will bucket
walkthrough.description: NTILE splits an ordered list into roughly equal buckets. Sort watch_seconds so bucket 1 holds the longest watches.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, watch_seconds FROM watch_events ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC, id LIMIT 12;

walkthrough.title: Assign quartile buckets
walkthrough.description: NTILE(4) labels rows 1–4 over the ordered window. Bucket edges can differ slightly when counts do not divide evenly.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, watch_seconds, NTILE(4) OVER(ORDER BY watch_seconds DESC, id) AS bucket FROM watch_events;

lessons.title: DDL: create, alter & inspect a table
lessons.concept: DDL changes structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML changes rows. Use the disposable lab to try both safely. Keep all statements in one script, ending with SELECT; the next execution starts fresh.
lessons.trap: Schema names and ALTER capabilities differ across engines.
hints: CREATE TABLE defines columns and constraints.
SQLite exposes a table-valued pragma_table_info function for this metadata.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Create practice_people with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and name TEXT; add city TEXT with ALTER TABLE. Return name and type from pragma_table_info('practice_people').
tasks.answer: CREATE TABLE practice_people(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,name TEXT); ALTER TABLE practice_people ADD COLUMN city TEXT; SELECT name,type FROM pragma_table_info('practice_people')

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM pragma_table_info('practice_people') WHERE (name='id' AND upper(type)='INTEGER' AND pk=1) OR (name='name' AND upper(type)='TEXT') OR (name='city' AND upper(type)='TEXT')

tasks.prompt: Create practice_totals with account_id INTEGER and total REAL. Return name and type from pragma_table_info('practice_totals').
tasks.answer: CREATE TABLE practice_totals(account_id INTEGER,total REAL); SELECT name,type FROM pragma_table_info('practice_totals')

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='table' AND name='practice_totals'

quiz.q: Which command changes structure rather than row contents?
quiz.why: ALTER is DDL; UPDATE and DELETE modify row contents.

walkthrough.title: Inspect the empty practice surface
walkthrough.description: DDL builds structure. Start from the lab items you already have, then create a separate practice table in the next step.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM lab_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Create and alter a table
walkthrough.description: CREATE TABLE defines columns; ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN extends the contract. Inspect with a SELECT afterward.

lessons.title: DML: INSERT, UPDATE & DELETE
lessons.concept: INSERT adds rows; UPDATE changes matching rows; DELETE removes matching rows. Use WHERE to constrain modifications. These exercises touch only disposable copies in memory and are reset on every run.
lessons.trap: An UPDATE without WHERE updates every row; that can be intentional only when the requirement says so.
hints: Use a WHERE clause on each targeted UPDATE and DELETE.
The base table starts with ids 1,2,3 on every execution.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Insert lab item (4, Pen, 8); add 5 to price for id=1; delete id=2. Return id, name, price for remaining items.
tasks.answer: INSERT INTO lab_items VALUES(4,'Pen',8); UPDATE lab_items SET price=price+5 WHERE id=1; DELETE FROM lab_items WHERE id=2; SELECT id,name,price FROM lab_items

tasks.prompt: Double every lab item price below 50, then delete items with price >100. Return id, name, price.
tasks.answer: UPDATE lab_items SET price=price*2 WHERE price<50; DELETE FROM lab_items WHERE price>100; SELECT id,name,price FROM lab_items

quiz.q: Why include a WHERE condition in a targeted UPDATE?
options: It limits which existing rows are changed
It guarantees a new row is inserted
quiz.why: UPDATE modifies matching rows. Without WHERE, every row is eligible; inspect the predicate before running a write.

walkthrough.title: Read rows before mutation
walkthrough.description: DML changes data. Note the current lab_items rows so you can see inserts, updates, and deletes afterward.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM lab_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Insert, update, then delete
walkthrough.description: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows, DELETE removes them. Run the full script to see the net effect.

lessons.title: Constraints protect the data contract
lessons.concept: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows; NOT NULL requires a value; UNIQUE prevents duplicate values; CHECK enforces a condition. SQLite CHECK passes NULL unless you also use NOT NULL. Foreign-key enforcement needs PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON; the lab enables it.
lessons.trap: These output exercises are followed by engine-level validation of the requested constraints.
hints: Declare constraints in the CREATE statement, not only in the SELECT.
Try a second run with a negative quantity or repeated email to see the engine reject it.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Create inventory with sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL and quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>=0); insert (A,2). Return sku and quantity.
tasks.answer: CREATE TABLE inventory(sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(quantity>=0)); INSERT INTO inventory VALUES('A',2); SELECT sku,quantity FROM inventory

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='table' AND name='inventory'
INSERT INTO inventory VALUES('B',-1)
INSERT INTO inventory VALUES('B',NULL)
INSERT INTO inventory VALUES('A',3)
INSERT INTO inventory VALUES(NULL,3)

tasks.prompt: Create contacts with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE; insert (1,a@example.com) and (2,b@example.com). Return id,email.
tasks.answer: CREATE TABLE contacts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE); INSERT INTO contacts VALUES(1,'a@example.com'),(2,'b@example.com'); SELECT id,email FROM contacts

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='table' AND name='contacts'
INSERT INTO contacts VALUES(3,'a@example.com')
INSERT INTO contacts VALUES(3,NULL)

quiz.q: Does CHECK(quantity>=0) alone forbid NULL in SQLite?
options: No; also use NOT NULL when missing quantity is invalid
quiz.why: CHECK passes NULL. NOT NULL is a separate constraint.

walkthrough.title: See data that constraints will protect
walkthrough.description: Constraints reject invalid writes. Think about NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY, and CHECK before creating inventory.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM lab_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Declare constraints on create
walkthrough.description: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, and CHECK(quantity >= 0) encode the data contract at write time.

lessons.title: Transactions & savepoint recovery
lessons.concept: A transaction groups changes. COMMIT keeps them in the current database; ROLLBACK undoes them. SAVEPOINT lets you undo a portion. In this app even committed changes vanish after the run because the entire database is disposable.
lessons.trap: A successful statement is not the same as a committed transaction.
hints: ROLLBACK undoes changes since BEGIN.
ROLLBACK TO partial preserves changes made before that savepoint.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Begin a transaction, add 10 to every lab item price, then roll back. Return id and price; all values should be original.
tasks.answer: BEGIN; UPDATE lab_items SET price=price+10; ROLLBACK; SELECT id,price FROM lab_items

tasks.prompt: Begin; add 5 to price for id=1; create SAVEPOINT partial; delete id=2; roll back to partial; commit. Return id and price.
tasks.answer: BEGIN; UPDATE lab_items SET price=price+5 WHERE id=1; SAVEPOINT partial; DELETE FROM lab_items WHERE id=2; ROLLBACK TO partial; COMMIT; SELECT id,price FROM lab_items

quiz.q: After ROLLBACK TO a savepoint, what happens to earlier transaction changes?
options: They remain pending in the transaction
quiz.why: A savepoint rollback undoes only later changes. COMMIT or full ROLLBACK still controls the transaction.

walkthrough.title: Note prices before a transaction
walkthrough.description: A transaction groups changes. ROLLBACK undoes them; COMMIT would keep them until this disposable database ends.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, price FROM lab_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Roll back a grouped change
walkthrough.description: BEGIN starts a transaction. After UPDATE, ROLLBACK restores the prior prices visible in the final SELECT.

lessons.title: Views: reusable query definitions
lessons.concept: A normal view is a named query definition. It is reusable without storing a snapshot of the result. A view can simplify business logic, but it is not automatically faster or slower than the equivalent query. SQLite views are read-only unless INSTEAD OF triggers support writes.
lessons.trap: A view is an abstraction, not a guarantee of materialization or caching.
hints: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ... stores the definition.
Query the new view in the same script.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Create view paid_orders exposing id, customer_id and quantity for paid orders. Return those columns by selecting the view.
tasks.answer: CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE status='paid'; SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM paid_orders

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='view' AND name='paid_orders'

tasks.prompt: Create view product_totals with category and total_price (sum of price). Return category and total_price from the view.
tasks.answer: CREATE VIEW product_totals AS SELECT category,SUM(price) AS total_price FROM products GROUP BY category; SELECT category,total_price FROM product_totals

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='view' AND name='product_totals'

quiz.q: What does a normal view store?
options: A snapshot of the rows at the moment you create it
A named query that runs when you select from it
Rows that exist only for the current connection
quiz.why: A view stores a query definition. Selecting from it runs that query against the current tables. It does not save a copy of the rows.

walkthrough.title: Look at the rows a view will read
walkthrough.description: A view does not copy these rows. It saves a query, and selecting the view reads the current orders.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, quantity, status FROM orders;

walkthrough.title: Execute a complete script
walkthrough.description: All setup and the final result run together in one disposable database.

lessons.title: CTEs, CTAS & temporary tables
lessons.concept: A CTE names an expression for one statement. A view persists a definition. CREATE TEMP TABLE ... AS SELECT materializes an intermediate result for the connection. SQL Server uses SELECT ... INTO #temp; that syntax is not SQLite. CTAS does not carry over source constraints.
lessons.trap: SQL Server CTEs do not materialize by default. SQLite can choose different CTE strategies; neither promises a universal speed-up.
hints: CREATE TEMP TABLE name AS SELECT ... builds the intermediate result.
The materialized result survives statements in this script, not future app runs.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Materialize a TEMP table customer_units with customer_id and total quantity as units. Return customer_id and units for units >3.
tasks.answer: CREATE TEMP TABLE customer_units AS SELECT customer_id,SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; SELECT customer_id,units FROM customer_units WHERE units>3

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_temp_schema WHERE name='customer_units' AND type='table'

tasks.prompt: Materialize a TEMP table category_prices with category and average price as avg_price. Return category and avg_price for avg_price >30.
tasks.answer: CREATE TEMP TABLE category_prices AS SELECT category,AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM products GROUP BY category; SELECT category,avg_price FROM category_prices WHERE avg_price>30

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_temp_schema WHERE name='category_prices' AND type='table'

quiz.q: Which object materializes its result for the current connection?
options: A temporary table created AS SELECT
quiz.why: A temp table stores intermediate rows. A view stores a query definition; SQL Server CTEs are not materialized results.

walkthrough.title: Compute units you will materialize
walkthrough.description: CTAS and TEMP tables store a query result. Build the customer_units shape in your head before writing CREATE TEMP TABLE.
walkthrough.query: SELECT customer_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Materialize with CTAS
walkthrough.description: CREATE TEMP TABLE … AS SELECT stores the result for later queries in the same session.

lessons.title: Triggers & visible audit effects
lessons.concept: A trigger runs automatically after a matching event. SQLite row triggers use OLD and NEW values. They can record an audit trail but also create hidden side effects. SQL Server triggers are statement-level and use inserted/deleted tables, so their code is different.
lessons.trap: A trigger’s side effect is part of the operation. Inspect and test it instead of assuming only one table changed.
hints: SQLite provides OLD.price, NEW.price and NEW.id inside the trigger.
CREATE TRIGGER contains BEGIN ... END; keep it intact in the script.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: Create a price_audit trigger AFTER UPDATE OF price on lab_items, logging changed prices in lab_audit; add 5 to id=1 price. Return item_id,old_price,new_price from lab_audit.
tasks.answer: CREATE TRIGGER price_audit AFTER UPDATE OF price ON lab_items WHEN OLD.price<>NEW.price BEGIN INSERT INTO lab_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); END; UPDATE lab_items SET price=price+5 WHERE id=1; SELECT item_id,old_price,new_price FROM lab_audit

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='trigger' AND name='price_audit'

tasks.prompt: Create the same trigger, then double prices for all items with price<50. Return item_id,old_price,new_price from lab_audit.
tasks.answer: CREATE TRIGGER price_audit AFTER UPDATE OF price ON lab_items WHEN OLD.price<>NEW.price BEGIN INSERT INTO lab_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); END; UPDATE lab_items SET price=price*2 WHERE price<50; SELECT item_id,old_price,new_price FROM lab_audit

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='trigger' AND name='price_audit'

quiz.q: When does an AFTER INSERT trigger run?
options: After each matching insertion into its table
Only when you manually query the trigger
Once when the table is created
quiz.why: The trigger runs in response to the declared table event. An audit trigger can insert a corresponding audit record automatically.

walkthrough.title: Read prices the trigger will watch
walkthrough.description: A trigger fires on a data change. Note current prices; an UPDATE that changes price should write an audit row.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, name, price FROM lab_items ORDER BY id;

walkthrough.title: Define a trigger and see its effect
walkthrough.description: AFTER UPDATE OF price inserts into an audit table when OLD.price differs from NEW.price.

lessons.title: Stored procedures: parameters & contracts
lessons.concept: A SQL Server stored procedure can expose parameters, transactions, and error handling. SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE. Here you practice the retrieval contract in SQLite; the separate T-SQL reference shows its SQL Server wrapper. Choose procedures or external orchestration based on the system, not a blanket preference.
lessons.example: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
lessons.trap: Parameters should be bound by a client or procedure, not concatenated from untrusted text.
hints: Treat the parameter as a defined input value.
The SQL Server wrapper is reference-only; run the retrieval query in this app.
lessons.grain: Each script starts from a fresh database and must end with a result query.

tasks.prompt: For customer_id=1, return id, customer_id and quantity from orders. This practices a procedure’s retrieval contract; no procedure is created in SQLite.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1

tasks.prompt: For customer_id=2, return id, customer_id and quantity for paid orders only.
tasks.answer: SELECT id,customer_id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=2 AND status='paid'

quiz.q: Can SQLite execute CREATE PROCEDURE from the T-SQL reference?
options: No; this lesson’s procedure wrapper is SQL Server reference only
quiz.why: The SQLite engine lacks stored procedures. Practice the retrieval contract here and the wrapper in SQL Server.

walkthrough.title: Call out the parameter boundary
walkthrough.description: Procedures package a contract: inputs in, result set out. Here the “parameter” is customer_id = 1 in the filter.
walkthrough.query: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;

walkthrough.title: Return rows for one parameter value
walkthrough.description: Filtering to a single customer_id models a parameterized lookup. Keep the contract explicit and narrow.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, customer_id, quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

lessons.title: Indexes: observe a real access path
lessons.concept: An index offers an access structure at the cost of storage and write work. Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to see SQLite choose SCAN, SEARCH, or a covering index. Plans describe physical access; they are not measured speed. This tiny dataset cannot establish a production performance improvement.
lessons.example:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;
lessons.trap: SQL Server clustered/nonclustered and columnstore indexes have different storage details from SQLite indexes.
hints: CREATE INDEX index_name ON table(column).
In lab mode Query plan runs setup statements, then explains the final SELECT.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.prompt: Create idx_orders_customer on orders(customer_id), then return id and quantity for customer_id=1. Run Query plan after the script to inspect the final SELECT.
tasks.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id); SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='index' AND name='idx_orders_customer'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM pragma_index_info('idx_orders_customer') WHERE name='customer_id'

tasks.prompt: Create idx_products_category on products(category), then return name and price for Tech products.
tasks.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products(category); SELECT name,price FROM products WHERE category='Tech'

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='index' AND name='idx_products_category'

quiz.q: An index changes SCAN to SEARCH on a tiny example. What can you conclude?
options: Production latency improved by a known percentage
The optimizer chose a different access path; measure the real workload next
quiz.why: A plan provides strategy evidence. Timing, reads, selectivity, and write overhead require workload measurement.

walkthrough.title: Plan a lookup before indexing
walkthrough.description: Without an index, filtering orders by customer_id may scan. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the current path.
walkthrough.query: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id, quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

walkthrough.title: Add an index and re-check the plan
walkthrough.description: CREATE INDEX can change the access path. Compare the new plan to the scan you saw before.
walkthrough.query:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id,quantity FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1;

lessons.title: SARGable ranges, not speed commandments
lessons.concept: A direct range on an indexed column can permit an efficient lookup. Wrapping that column in a function can prevent a normal index lookup; expression indexes are a separate option. Compare real plans and preserve the result. OR, correlated subqueries, and joins are not universally slow.
lessons.trap: SARGability makes an index strategy possible; statistics, selectivity, and workload determine whether it wins.
hints: Use >= start and < the next boundary without wrapping watched_at.
Inspect the plan; do not infer speed just from the SQL spelling.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.prompt: Create idx_watch_time on watched_at; return id and watched_at for Jan 2025 using a half-open timestamp range.
tasks.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_watch_time ON watch_events(watched_at); SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at>='2025-01-01' AND watched_at<'2025-02-01'

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='index' AND name='idx_watch_time'

tasks.prompt: Create idx_watch_time on watched_at; return id and watched_at for Jan 1–7 2025 inclusive, using a half-open range.
tasks.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_watch_time ON watch_events(watched_at); SELECT id,watched_at FROM watch_events WHERE watched_at>='2025-01-01' AND watched_at<'2025-01-08'

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type='index' AND name='idx_watch_time'

quiz.q: Which filter can search an index on watched_at?
options: A half-open range written on watched_at itself
A function wrapped around watched_at, such as date(watched_at)
A comparison that never mentions watched_at
quiz.why: A range on the bare column can SEARCH an index. Wrapping the column in a function often forces a scan unless you add an expression index.

walkthrough.title: Filter the timestamp column directly
walkthrough.description: watched_at is the column an index can search. Wrapping it in a function is a different question.
walkthrough.query: SELECT id, watched_at FROM watch_events ORDER BY watched_at LIMIT 8;

walkthrough.title: Execute a complete script
walkthrough.description: All setup and the final result run together in one disposable database.

lessons.title: Partitioning & workload trade-offs
lessons.concept: Partitioning splits a large table by a defined key. It can aid pruning and lifecycle management, but is not a universal query accelerator. SQLite has no SQL Server partition function/scheme. Practice time-aligned filtering here; use the reference notes to understand native warehouse partitioning.
lessons.example:
SELECT sale_key,order_date,sales FROM fact_sales
WHERE order_date>='2025-02-01' AND order_date<'2025-03-01';
lessons.trap: Partitioning and clustering are different. Do not report partition elimination from a SQLite plan.
hints: The filter should align with the hypothetical date partition key.
Inspect time boundaries and the result; there are no physical partitions in this engine.
lessons.grain: Measure a defined result, then inspect the physical strategy.

tasks.prompt: Return sale_key, order_date and sales for Feb 2025 from fact_sales. Use a half-open range.
tasks.answer: SELECT sale_key,order_date,sales FROM fact_sales WHERE order_date>='2025-02-01' AND order_date<'2025-03-01'

tasks.prompt: Return month (YYYY-MM) and sales (sum) by month from fact_sales.
tasks.answer: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m',order_date) AS month,SUM(sales) AS sales FROM fact_sales GROUP BY month

quiz.q: Does this SQLite example prove physical partition elimination?
options: No; it has no SQL Server native partitions
Only if the result has one month
quiz.why: A time predicate is transferable; physical partition schemes and pruning are engine-specific.

walkthrough.title: Filter a date slice of the fact
walkthrough.description: Partitioning ideas show up as pruning a date range. Narrow fact_sales to one month before aggregating.

walkthrough.title: Query within the partition window
walkthrough.description: Date predicates that match partition boundaries let engines skip irrelevant slices. Keep the range half-open.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT sale_key,order_date,sales FROM fact_sales
WHERE order_date>='2025-02-01' AND order_date<'2025-03-01';

lessons.title: Bronze: inspect raw data before cleaning
lessons.concept: Bronze preserves source records for traceability. Profile missing keys, duplicates, dates, and type mismatches before writing cleaning rules. Do not silently erase rows without documenting why. These source rows are fictional, inspired by common CRM/catalog/sales issues.
lessons.trap: A date parse check is not a complete calendar validation policy; production rules must also define format and acceptable ranges.
hints: Normalize a key for profiling without changing the original rows.
Use a group count for duplicates and date(...) IS NULL for the provided invalid-date case.
lessons.grain: Respect the sales-line grain and use dimension keys for relationships.

tasks.prompt: Return customer_id (trimmed raw_id) and versions for non-NULL duplicate customer keys in bronze_customers. Keep only keys with more than one version.
tasks.answer: SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,COUNT(*) AS versions FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY TRIM(raw_id) HAVING COUNT(*)>1

tasks.prompt: Return row_id and order_date for bronze sales whose date is invalid (date(order_date) IS NULL).
tasks.answer: SELECT row_id,order_date FROM bronze_sales WHERE date(order_date) IS NULL

quiz.q: Why keep invalid and duplicate records in Bronze while profiling them?
options: So every record automatically belongs in reports
To preserve source evidence and explain later cleaning decisions
quiz.why: Bronze preserves traceable source records. Profiling identifies quality issues before explicit cleaning or quarantine rules are applied.

walkthrough.title: Preserve the raw input
walkthrough.description: Note duplicate C001, spaces, and the missing key.
walkthrough.query: SELECT * FROM bronze_customers;

walkthrough.title: Profile duplicates
walkthrough.description: Normalize keys for analysis without modifying the Bronze table.
walkthrough.query: SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,COUNT(*) AS versions FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY TRIM(raw_id) HAVING COUNT(*)>1

walkthrough.title: Inspect rejected dates
walkthrough.description: The invalid source row remains traceable.
walkthrough.query: SELECT row_id,order_date FROM bronze_sales WHERE date(order_date) IS NULL

lessons.title: Silver: clean, map & deduplicate
lessons.concept: Silver applies explicit quality rules. Normalize keys and text, keep the latest customer version, map country codes, and exclude missing keys. With equal version timestamps production logic needs an additional reliable tie-breaker; this sample has none.
lessons.example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE silver_customers AS WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY TRIM(raw_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(raw_id)<>'') SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,TRIM(name) AS name,CASE UPPER(TRIM(country)) WHEN 'US' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'GB' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'IND' THEN 'India' WHEN 'CA' THEN 'Canada' ELSE UPPER(TRIM(country)) END AS country FROM ranked WHERE rn=1;
SELECT customer_id,name,country FROM silver_customers;
lessons.trap: Keep the source unchanged and make exclusion rules visible. A new surrogate key is not a substitute for deduplication.
hints: ROW_NUMBER partitions on the normalized natural key.
Keep rn=1, then trim and map the surviving rows.
lessons.grain: Respect the sales-line grain and use dimension keys for relationships.

tasks.prompt: Create TEMP silver_customers: trim keys/names; discard NULL/empty keys; keep latest updated_at per trimmed key. Map US/USA→United States, GB/UK→United Kingdom, IND→India, CA→Canada. Return customer_id,name,country.
tasks.answer: CREATE TEMP TABLE silver_customers AS WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY TRIM(raw_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(raw_id)<>'') SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,TRIM(name) AS name,CASE UPPER(TRIM(country)) WHEN 'US' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'GB' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'IND' THEN 'India' WHEN 'CA' THEN 'Canada' ELSE UPPER(TRIM(country)) END AS country FROM ranked WHERE rn=1; SELECT customer_id,name,country FROM silver_customers

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_temp_schema WHERE name='silver_customers' AND type='table'

tasks.prompt: Create the same TEMP silver_customers, then return country and customer_count per mapped country.
tasks.answer: CREATE TEMP TABLE silver_customers AS WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY TRIM(raw_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(raw_id)<>'') SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,TRIM(name) AS name,CASE UPPER(TRIM(country)) WHEN 'US' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'GB' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'IND' THEN 'India' WHEN 'CA' THEN 'Canada' ELSE UPPER(TRIM(country)) END AS country FROM ranked WHERE rn=1; SELECT country,COUNT(*) AS customer_count FROM silver_customers GROUP BY country

validate.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sqlite_temp_schema WHERE name='silver_customers' AND type='table'

quiz.q: After TRIM and ROW_NUMBER per raw_id ordered by updated_at descending, why keep only rn = 1?
options: To invent a new surrogate warehouse key on every load
To keep the latest cleaned version of each natural key
To drop every row that ever had a duplicate
quiz.why: Silver normalizes and deduplicates source versions. Ordering newest-first and keeping rn = 1 retains one current row per trimmed key. Surrogate keys belong to later Gold modeling.

walkthrough.title: Profile duplicate natural keys
walkthrough.description: Bronze keeps every source version. Silver will trim keys, map countries, and keep the latest updated_at per key.
walkthrough.query:
SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id, COUNT(*) AS versions
FROM bronze_customers
WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY TRIM(raw_id)
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

walkthrough.title: Execute a complete script
walkthrough.description: All setup and the final result run together in one disposable database.
walkthrough.query:
CREATE TEMP TABLE silver_customers AS WITH ranked AS(SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY TRIM(raw_id) ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM bronze_customers WHERE raw_id IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(raw_id)<>'') SELECT TRIM(raw_id) AS customer_id,TRIM(name) AS name,CASE UPPER(TRIM(country)) WHEN 'US' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'United States' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'GB' THEN 'United Kingdom' WHEN 'IND' THEN 'India' WHEN 'CA' THEN 'Canada' ELSE UPPER(TRIM(country)) END AS country FROM ranked WHERE rn=1;

lessons.title: Gold: dimensions, facts & quality gates

lessons.title: Validate calendar dates before converting
lessons.concept: Eight digits do not prove a valid date. Shape YYYYMMDD to YYYY-MM-DD, require exactly eight digits, and compare the candidate to SQLite date(candidate,+0 days) so normalization exposes impossible dates. Invalid or missing values remain NULL; keep the source row. SQL Server uses TRY_CONVERT with an explicit style.

hints: Use an eight-position digit GLOB pattern rather than CAST alone.
date(candidate,'+0 days') must equal candidate. Equality with NULL will not pass WHEN.
lessons.grain: Declare the source grain, normalization rule, and target contract. Every write run is disposable.
